en: The Scripture on Upholding the World, Scroll One.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The First Chapter of the Scripture on Upholding the World.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha together with a great community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by several hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings who paid him respectful homage as he preached the Dharma for them.

In that assembly was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dharaṇīśvara (Holding the World), who, for the sake of the immeasurable merit-adornments of the resolve of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, desired to thoroughly know the further shore of all dharmas; desired to thoroughly know how to give rise to immeasurable vows and fulfill immeasurable adornments; desired to penetrate the definitive characteristics of immeasurable dharmas; desired to give rise to immeasurable adorned vows and purify the conduct of the profound mind; desired to thoroughly know pure and complete generosity; desired to thoroughly know definitively pure upholding of the precepts; desired to thoroughly know the mind of patience and suppleness endowed with fulfillment; desired to thoroughly know pure diligence; desired to thoroughly know pure meditative concentration; and desired to thoroughly know the penetration of the further shore of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
By virtue of such immeasurable merits as these, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I wish to question the Buddha for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, as well as to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas; those who possess full dignity and proper conduct while remaining unattached to the observance of precepts, who are endowed with pure discipline and practice the Great Dharma, and who skillfully know how to maintain the path of immeasurable spheres of conduct.

For the sake of these bodhisattvas, I now ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One: how is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to skillfully know the true reality of all phenomena, and also skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all teachings?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the power of mindfulness, and furthermore, transform their rebirth so as to achieve uninterrupted mindfulness until they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Lokadhara, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Lokadhara!

Since you are able to ask the Tathāgata about this matter for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, you should know that you bring great peace and security to sentient beings, have compassion for the world, and benefit, bring joy to, and provide peace for gods and humans alike. Furthermore, you act as a great light for all bodhisattvas of the present and future; your merit is immeasurable.”

That you are able to ask the Tathāgata such a matter, it is because you surely desire to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, to love and protect all sentient beings, and to act as their light; because you wish to show sentient beings what is meaningful and beneficial, and wish to enable them to cross over the perilous path; because you wish to be a refuge, a dwelling, an island, and a savior for sentient beings; because you wish to uproot sentient beings from the three evil realms and establish them in the unsurpassed path; because you wish to liberate sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; because you wish to grant sentient beings the bliss of unsurpassed nirvāṇa; and because you wish to protect the True Dharma in future ages, and to deliver sentient beings during the terrors of future degenerate times.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Listen now well and reflect upon it with care; I shall explain this matter for you.
“So be it, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Dhāraṇīdhara:
“Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive four benefits, they diligently cultivate the true mark of all dharmas and also skillfully discern the phrases and chapters of all dharmas.”
What are the four?
One shall attain full mindfulness; one shall attain uninterrupted mindfulness; one shall cause mindfulness to increase through settled wisdom; and mindfulness shall always abide in the mind.
"World-Holder!

It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see these four benefits that they diligently cultivate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and also skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all teachings."
“Lokadhara!

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see four benefits, whereby they diligently cultivate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and also skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all teachings.

What are the four? They are: one should skillfully know the definitive meaning of all phenomena; one should skillfully know the meanings of all phenomena; one should skillfully know the various causes and conditions of all phenomena; and one should skillfully enter the gateway to the reality of all phenomena. These are the four.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see four benefits for which they diligently cultivate the true mark of all dharmas and skillfully discern the phrases and chapters of all dharmas.

What are the four? One should skillfully know the characteristics of immeasurable dharmas; one should cultivate the skillful knowledge of the certainty of immeasurable dharmas; one should practice immeasurable merits so as to increase oneself; and one should know and see the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all dharmas. These are the four.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see four benefits, whereby they diligently cultivate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and also skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all teachings.”
What are the four?

One shall draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one shall swiftly fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment; one shall not follow the words of others because of being well-versed in the skillful means (*upāya*) regarding all phenomena; and one shall be well-versed in all wisdom.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

It is for the sake of seeing these four benefits that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently cultivate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and also skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently cultivate the true mark of all dharmas and also skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.”
What are the four? They are:

having a mind free from the stain of stinginess for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; constantly practicing pure precepts and abiding in the *vīrya-pāramitā*; initiating and exerting diligence without ceasing or resting; and skillfully practicing the *prajñā-pāramitā* through right reflection. These are the four.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently cultivate the true mark of all dharmas and also skillfully discern the phrases and chapters of all dharmas.”

What are the four? They are: the fulfillment of the vow of a profoundly pure deep mind; the fulfillment and accomplishment of the merit of pure conduct; abiding in the merit of gentleness and patience; and attaining the light that discerns the true reality of all phenomena. These are the four.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivates the true mark of all dharmas and also skillfully discerns the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are the four? They are:

seeking all-knowledge with great aspiration; generating great aspiration through skillfully knowing and discerning dhyānas, liberations, and various samādhis; practicing the sphere of pure conduct through the desire to attain the minds of great kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; and skillfully cultivating the definitive meaning. These are the four.
“World-Upholder!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivates the true mark of all dharmas and also skillfully discerns the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are the four? They are:
being fully endowed with the practice of wisdom; seeking the sphere of pure gnosis; delighting in unimpeded knowledge; and never being separated from the aspiration for all-encompassing wisdom.
“World-Upholder!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivates the true mark of all dharmas and is also skilled in discerning the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.”
“Holder of the World!
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees four benefits, he is able to seek the power of mindfulness.
What are these four?

One should cultivate and fulfill the faculty of mindfulness; one should practice settled wisdom; one should possess uninterrupted mindfulness; and one should cultivate and fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness—these are the four.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees four benefits that enable him to seek the power of mindfulness.
What are these four?

Because they are fully endowed with all the factors conducive to enlightenment, mindfulness is always present in their minds; because they skillfully cultivate and accumulate the faculty of mindfulness, they master the recollection of past lives; and because they are fully endowed with pure wisdom, they shall swiftly attain uninterrupted mindfulness and plant the causal conditions for all-encompassing wisdom—these are the four.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees four benefits that enable him to seek the power of mindfulness.
What are these four?

One should cultivate and perfect the skillful means of contemplation; one should practice wisdom according to reality; one should exert diligent effort in order to attain all Buddha-dharmas; and one should maintain mindfulness without forgetting in order to attain uninterrupted power of recollection.
“World-Upholder!
It is because they see these four benefits that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to seek the power of mindfulness.
World-Upholder!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess four dharmas by which they are able to attain the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*).
What are these four? They are:

constant diligent application of effort without ceasing or resting because they maintain settled wisdom; constantly unifying the mind to realize the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; constant non-negligence through right mindfulness of all phenomena; and constant guarding of the sense faculties through right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). These are the four.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can attain the power of mindfulness.
What are these four?

To abide securely in pure ethical discipline; to accomplish pure conduct and deportment; to remove the five hindrances from the mind; and to remain unstained by worldly dharmas while being free from karmic obstructions and afflictive obstructions—these are the four.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can attain the power of mindfulness.
What are these four?

Seeking wholesome dharmas with an undistracted mind; diligently practicing the state of single-mindedness; skillfully knowing how to correctly enter the various gateways of the Dharma; and not delighting in clamor while remaining far removed from household life—these are the four.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be able to attain the power of mindfulness.
What are these four?

One should draw near to spiritual friends, constantly practice the profound Dharma, always delight in going to the abodes of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and always delight in inquiring about and practicing wisdom.
“World-Holder!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have attained the power of mindfulness.
World-Holder!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive four benefits, they are able to cultivate the wisdom that discriminates the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.

What are these four? They are: they shall thoroughly know the true mark of all dharmas; they shall discriminate the causes of all dharmas; they shall know the definitive meaning of all dharmas; and they shall thoroughly know the words, chapters, and phrases of all dharmas. These are the four.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see four kinds of benefit, they are able to cultivate and accumulate the wisdom that discerns the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are these four?

One should skillfully know the sequential order of all phenomena as appropriate; one should skillfully know the expedient means of the causes and conditions of all phenomena; one should fully cultivate and accumulate the expedient means of all phenomena; and one should discern and understand sūtras of definitive meaning and those of non-definitive meaning—these are the four.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees four kinds of benefits, they are able to cultivate and accumulate the wisdom that discerns the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are these four?

One should skillfully train in this wisdom that distinguishes between the path and what is not the path; one should attain the power of eloquence in explaining the meaning of all dharmas; one should swiftly attain the sphere of pure wisdom; and one should fully cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“World-Upholder!
These are the four benefits that a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees,
by which they are able to cultivate and collect the wisdom that discriminates the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.”
“World-Upholder!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cultivate and collect the wisdom that discriminates all dharmas and their phrases.”
What are the four? They are:

skillfully knowing the characteristics of the accumulation of all phenomena; skillfully knowing the characteristics of the cessation of the causes of all phenomena; skillfully knowing the characteristics of the conditions of all phenomena; and being able to enter the skillful means of dependent origination. These are the four.
“World-Upholder!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cultivate and collect the wisdom that discriminates the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are these four?

Skillfully knowing the suffering of all phenomena, skillfully knowing the origin of all phenomena, skillfully knowing the cessation of all phenomena, and skillfully knowing the path leading to the cessation of all phenomena—these are the four.
"World-Upholder!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cultivate and collect the wisdom that discriminates the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are these four? They are:

skillfully knowing the expedient means of the conjunction and dispersal of all dharmas; attaining the power of prior causes; skillfully knowing what is appropriate for all dharmas; and skillfully knowing how to discriminate written characters and phrases. These are the four.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cultivate and accumulate the wisdom that discerns the chapters and phrases of all dharmas.
What are these four?

They skillfully understand the sutras of provisional meaning; regarding the sutras of definitive meaning, they do not rely on the words of others; they skillfully understand the seal of the characteristics of all phenomena, and they also skillfully abide in the wisdom of the signlessness of all phenomena.
“World-Holder!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to cultivate and collect the wisdom that discriminates all dharmas and their phrases and sentences.
World-Holder!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four dharmas by which, upon changing bodies, they always attain uninterrupted mindfulness until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these four?

To clearly understand wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; to achieve the foremost mindfulness, tranquility, and wisdom; to be able to free the mind from the five hindrances; and never to forget the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—these are the four.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon changing bodies, always attains uninterrupted mindfulness until he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the four? They are:

skillfully cultivating and accumulating the four foundations of mindfulness; skillfully cultivating and accumulating the wisdom of analytical discernment; making wisdom the foremost among all meditative concentrations; and attaining penetration within definitive wisdom. These are the four.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon changing bodies, always attains uninterrupted mindfulness until he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the four?
Attaining the gates of all dhāraṇīs, cultivating and accumulating the wisdom of non-arising, entering the wisdom of exhaustion, and contemplating the wisdom of cessation—these are the four.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon changing bodies, constantly attains uninterrupted mindfulness until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are the four? They are:
severing craving and aversion; not being greedily attached to any conditioned phenomena; the mind penetrating the wisdom of the unconditioned; and reaching the sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity.
“World-Upholder!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon changing bodies, always attains uninterrupted mindfulness until they attain the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five powers of pure wisdom through which they are able to fully attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of wisdom that purifies the profound mind, the power of wisdom that purifies vows, the power of wisdom that purifies roots of goodness, the power of wisdom that purifies dedication, and the power of wisdom that purifies obstructive karma—these are the five.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five powers of pure wisdom, by means of which they are fully able to attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of pure wisdom regarding the purity of deportment and conduct; the power of pure wisdom regarding the fulfillment of mindfulness; the power of pure wisdom regarding skillful means; the power of pure wisdom regarding the focus on sentient beings; and the power of pure wisdom regarding the focus on signs—these are the five.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five purifying powers of wisdom (*jñānabala*) by which they are able to fully attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of wisdom that purifies the mind of equanimity; the power of wisdom that benefits sentient beings; the power of wisdom that gives rise to great loving-kindness; the power of wisdom that gives rise to great compassion; and the power of wisdom that gives rise to great sympathetic joy and great equanimity—these are the five.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five purifying powers of wisdom, by which they are able to fully attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of purity through maintaining the precepts, the power of purity through non-attachment to maintaining the precepts; the power of purity through patience, the power of purity through non-attachment to patience; and the power of purity through extensive learning—these are the five.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five purifying powers of wisdom, by means of which they are able to fully attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of purity through profound diligence, the power of purity through receptive diligence, the power of purity through meditative concentration, the power of purity through the skillful means of meditative concentration, and the power of purity through the skillful means of tranquility and insight—these are the five.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, there are five powers of pure wisdom possessed by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, all of which enable them to fully attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of wisdom-purity; the power of wisdom-purity through the skillful means of certainty based on extensive learning; the power of wisdom-purity regarding the mundane and the supramundane; the power of wisdom-purity through skillful means; and the power of wisdom-purity regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned—these are the five.
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess five kinds of pure power of wisdom, by which they are able to fully attain the aforementioned merits.
What are these five?

The power of wisdom that purifies through skillful means; the power of wisdom that purifies through clear liberation; the power of wisdom that purifies through the mark of non-arising; the power of wisdom that purifies through the single mark of signlessness; and the power of wisdom that purifies through the meanings of the ultimate truth and conventional truth.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to possess these five powers of pure wisdom, by which they swiftly attain the full completion of all such merits.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra!”
For this benefit, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should diligently cultivate and accumulate within this power of pure wisdom.
"Sustainer of the World!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes three dharmas, they are able to diligently cultivate and accumulate within this power of pure wisdom."
What are these three?

First, desire; second, diligence; and third, heedfulness. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these three dharmas, they are able to diligently cultivate and accumulate [virtues] within this power of pure wisdom that is fully endowed with all merits.
Why is this so? Holder of the World!
Desire, diligence, and non-negligence are the roots of all dharmas.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains this power of pure wisdom, they are able to swiftly attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). They are called one who is diligent and non-regressive, and also called one whose dharma is non-regressive. Furthermore, by means of these merits, they swiftly achieve growth, and they swiftly attain the power of pure wisdom regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
“Holder of the World!

If there is anyone who attains pure power of wisdom regarding all these dharmas, this person is a field of merit for the world; such a person can receive offerings next to me; such a person can reach the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice; such a person can contemplate the Dharma of the Tathāgata; and such a person will before long be able to realize the wisdom of the Tathāgata.”
“Holder of the World!
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction:
‘After immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall attain buddhahood.’”
Immediately, he attained such power of pure wisdom through universal knowledge. "Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
If there should be anyone who can achieve such power of pure wisdom regarding all dharmas, that person shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, just as I have now attained it."
This person also turns the wheel of Dharma just as I do now;
this person also roars the lion’s roar just as I do now;
this person also attains sovereign power over all dharmas just as I do now.
“World-Upholder!
You all should apply yourselves with diligent vigor within this power of pure wisdom; before long, you will naturally become fully endowed with all-encompassing wisdom.
World-Upholder!”

In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Jñānottararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
“World-Upholder!

This Tathāgata King of Exalted Wisdom has an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas and also an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas; this is brought about by the causal conditions of that Buddha’s original vows.”

In the buddha-field of the Buddha Jñānottama, there are no three evil realms; its sentient beings do not perceive suffering, but are ultimately endowed with peace, security, and happiness. Those who have largely abandoned desire are able to obstruct the five hindrances.
These sentient beings achieve such pure happiness as that experienced by one who has entered the fourth dhyāna.
The lifespan of this Buddha Jñānottara-rāja was six million billion nayutas of kalpas.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! At that time, in that land, the Buddha alone shall be the king; there will be no other king, and the sentient beings of that land shall all address the Buddha as the Dharma King.

This Buddha Jñānottara-rāja will extensively preach for the sake of the bodhisattvas this *Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra*, which severs all doubts of sentient beings and gladdens the hearts of all sentient beings.”

At that time, there were five hundred bodhisattvas who, having heard of this pure power of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, exerted such power of diligence that for the rest of their lives they never gave rise to the thought of sitting down; for the rest of their lives they never gave rise to thoughts of clothing; for the rest of their lives they never gave rise to thoughts of self, thoughts of sentient beings, thoughts of persons, or thoughts of male or female; and for the rest of their lives they never ate much, but instead cultivated and accumulated this pure power of wisdom, practicing with diligent vigor.

By reason of these roots of goodness, five hundred bodhisattvas, at the end of their lives, were all reborn beyond one hundred trillion lands to the east. Not long after their birth, because they had cultivated and accumulated this Dharma, they attained the recollection of past lives and achieved sharp faculties.

In that land, the Buddha is named King of Immeasurable Flower Accumulations, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma. His bodhisattvas are sixteen years of age when they leave the household life under King of Immeasurable Flower Accumulations Buddha; for sixty billion years they practice the celibate conduct of a youth, cultivating such diligence as this.
“Holder of the World!

These five hundred bodhisattvas encountered twenty billion buddhas such as these, and under those buddhas they practiced with diligent perseverance. They accomplished the foremost mindfulness of peaceful wisdom, and finally encountered the Buddha Immeasurable Power High King, who bestowed upon them the prediction that after ten thousand kalpas had passed, they would attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

These five hundred people, throughout ten thousand kalpas, shall encounter twenty trillion Buddhas and fulfill the path of Buddhahood; within a single kalpa, they shall successively attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
You should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should, within this power of pure wisdom, give rise to desire, diligence, and heedfulness.”
Why is this? World-Holder!

The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas has desire, diligence, and heedfulness as its root, as well as other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which enable one to fulfill the Buddha-dharmas.
“Holder of the World!

Through such diligence, I encountered two billion buddhas; in every lifetime among all dharmas, I accomplished the power of mindfulness, and in every lifetime I attained the knowledge of past lives. I cultivated and gathered these dharmas without ceasing or resting, never losing this desire, diligence, and heedfulness, and I shall surely accomplish desire, diligence, and heedfulness.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, with a heart of great compassion, surveyed the four quarters and manifested supernatural powers, causing transformed Buddhas to appear in every Jambudvīpa throughout the trichiliocosm, preaching for the sake of all sentient beings this *Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra*, which Severs All Doubts of Sentient Beings and Gladdens the Hearts of All Sentient Beings.
Furthermore, by means of his supernatural power, he caused the great assembly gathered in the Bamboo Grove to see all the Buddhas throughout Jambudvīpa, each preaching the Dharma.
The assembly was filled with joy; they rose from their seats, prostrated together before the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
"The spiritual powers of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are inconceivable; they have accomplished immeasurable, inconceivable dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"O sons of good family!
For the Tathāgata, this matter is not difficult.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is perfectly able to penetrate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

If the power of supernormal transformations were to issue from a single pore, its radiance would universally illumine worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions and it would proclaim the sounds of the Dharma; yet even this would not exhaust one hundred thousand million billionth part of what issues from a single pore. Such are the inconceivable merits accomplished by the Tathāgata.
“O sons of good family!
The Tathāgata observes the minds of sentient beings with profound insight and teaches them the Dharma accordingly.
O sons of good family!”
In this world, few among sentient beings are able to practice with joyful desire for this Dharma.
O sons of good family!
In this world, few among sentient beings are able to practice with diligence for this Dharma.
"O sons of good family!
Among the sentient beings of the present age, few are able to practice heedfulness within this Dharma. Why is this?"

The Tathāgata has now appeared in this world of the five turbidities—namely, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of lifespan, the turbidity of afflictions, and the turbidity of the eon.
O sons of good family!
If there were even a single person who could believe and accept such a profound and pure Dharma and reach the wisdom of the Buddha, that would be rare indeed!
How much more so for one who can believe and understand the conduct of the Tathāgata?
“O sons of good family!

For a long night, I have constantly adorned myself with such vows, and practiced such diligence and patience, for the sake of sentient beings who are suffering, who have no protector, who have no refuge, and who have mostly fallen into the evil realms; at that time, I shall attain the Way of the Buddha and benefit immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings.”
"O sons of good family!

You should know that the power of the Tathāgata’s grace is fundamentally pure; because of his vow and diligence, he is able to cause immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings to believe, understand, and uphold such profound Dharma."
“O sons of good family!
In previous lives, I taught and transformed sentient beings, and these sentient beings were able to understand my Dharma.
O sons of good family!”
Now, by means of the ten powers and four fearlessnesses, the Buddha is able to inspire even a few sentient beings to have faith and understanding in such a profound Dharma.
If there are sentient beings who abide within this Dharma, it is entirely due to the power of the Tathāgata’s grace and skillful means.

For a long night I have not been separated from such profound dharmas; for a long night I have also embraced sentient beings with great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
Rarely does a Tathāgata appear in an age of five turbidities to benefit sentient beings.
Why is this? Sons of good family!
In previous lives, through the power of great diligence and the power of great skillful means, I taught and transformed sentient beings, thereby accumulating this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“O sons of good family!
I recall that in a past life, within a single day, I sacrificed a thousand bodies in giving to benefit sentient beings.
O sons of good family!”

Throughout many tens of millions of lifetimes, because I saw sentient beings suffering from hunger, I have cut the flesh from my own body and boiled it to give to them; at those times, my mind was free from sorrow or regret, for I practiced great compassion universally toward all sentient beings.
"O sons of good family!

You should know that it was by means of such great diligence and the power of great skillful means that I have taught and transformed sentient beings, thereby accumulating this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Therefore, sons of good family!

You should give rise to such desire, diligence, and heedfulness to cultivate and accumulate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Just as I practiced the bodhisattva path, you too should benefit and transform sentient beings just as I have done.
“O sons of good family!
Among all the Buddhas who have appeared in this Bhadrakalpa, there are none who have not praised me, speaking thus:
‘Śākyamuni Buddha has practiced such profound diligence; Śākyamuni Buddha is endowed with such perfection of diligence; Śākyamuni Buddha is fully possessed of such a pāramitā of diligence.’”

When Śākyamuni Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he taught and transformed sentient beings in this manner, emerging from the five turbidities to benefit immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.
"O sons of good family!
Because one practices the path in this manner, you should diligently give rise to aspiration, vigor, and heedfulness.
O sons of good family!"

Although I have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my vigor still does not rest; even until the time of nirvāṇa, I shall continue to exert vigor, breaking my body’s bones into pieces as small as mustard seeds and dissolving my limbs and joints.
Why is this? It is because of compassion for sentient beings of future ages.

When I was practicing the bodhisattva path in previous lives, there were sentient beings whom I had transformed who, having committed errors in their conduct, fell into various states of suffering. Desiring to rescue and deliver them, I gave rise to great compassion and distributed my relics—even those as small as mustard seeds—endowing them all with supernatural power.

After my parinirvāṇa, if there are sentient beings who should be delivered by means of relics so that their minds attain purity, and having attained such purity, they shall achieve their vows in every place upon the earth.
“O sons of good family!

When I practiced the Way in past lives, I cultivated such a heart of compassion among sentient beings that I caused my fragmented bodily relics to be distributed everywhere; this was my original vow.”
"By means of such immeasurable causes and conditions of merit and through my heart of great compassion, I shall universally shelter all sentient beings in the future evil age.
O sons of good family!

If there are bodhisattvas who, within this Dharma, are able to give rise to desire, diligence, and heedfulness, they shall certainly make this vow: "In the future final age, I shall receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain such sūtras as these for others. I, by means of my supernormal powers, shall cause those bodhisattvas to receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain them for others; I also entrust these sūtras to those bodhisattvas because they are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain them for others.
Why is this so? Sons of good family!
Wherever this sutra abides, you should know that in that land the Buddha has not passed into extinction; for this reason, the Tathāgata entrusts this sutra to all bodhisattvas.
“O sons of good family!

You should know that in past lives I gathered in sentient beings through such causes and conditions; in this present life I likewise gather in sentient beings, and in future lives I shall likewise gather in sentient beings—namely, by protecting and mindful of this Dharma of the sutra so that it may be widely disseminated during the final five hundred years.”
“O sons of good family!

Whether in this present age or after my parinirvāṇa, whether in villages, cities, towns, mountain forests, or wildernesses, wherever such sūtras as these exist, and whoever is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain them for others, you should know that a Buddha is present therein.”
Why is this? I say that all Buddhas are the Dharma-body; because one sees the Dharma, one sees the Buddha. A Buddha should not be seen by means of the form-body (rūpakāya).
If a person has faith in the Dharma and listens to the Dharma, that person is one who has faith in the Buddha and also listens to the Buddha’s words.

If a person is able to practice according to what is taught within this Dharma, that person is one who sees the Buddha; such a person is called a speaker of truth, a speaker of the Dharma, and a follower of the Dharma.
“O sons of good family!

My body is neither dharma nor non-dharma; this is called ‘practice in accordance with the Dharma,’ and it is called the foremost gift of Dharma—namely, non-attachment to dharma and non-attachment to non-dharma.”
Why is this? Those who are attached to dharmas are not said to see the Buddha.
"O sons of good family!
To be unattached to all phenomena is called seeing the Buddha.
If one perceives nothing within all phenomena, this is called seeing the Buddha. Why is this?
The Tathāgata cannot be described by means of dharmas, nor can he be described by means of non-dharmas, nor can he be seen by means of dharmas. Why is this so?
O sons of good family!
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣus!
If you understand my Dharma to be like the simile of a raft, then even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
If one can relinquish both the Dharma and non-Dharma, this is called seeing the Buddha. Why is this?
The Tathāgata is named the one who has relinquished all dharmas; he does not crave or grasp at the names of any dharmas, nor does he fall into the dharmas of names.
How much less could one fall into the names and designations of what is not the Dharma?
"O sons of good family!
To abandon all names and designations of dharmas is called the Tathāgata; those who can see in this way are said to see the Tathāgata."
Why is this? Because one abandons the view of all phenomena, it is called "seeing the Tathāgata," for all phenomena are unattainable.
Because one knows and sees all phenomena as they truly are, it is called "seeing the Tathāgata."
“O sons of good family!

If all dharmas are unattainable and one has relinquished all dharmas, therein there is no conceptual proliferation; there are no names of ‘dharma’ or ‘non-dharma,’ no practice, and no demonstration—this is called seeing the Tathāgata.”
If a person can see the Dharma in this way, they are said to see the Tathāgata.
If one can see the Tathāgata in this way, it is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
To see otherwise is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); if one holds wrong view, it is a deluded view, and such a person is not said to have true vision.
“O sons of good family!

Those who see truly cut off all paths of speech; they are neither true nor false, neither existent nor non-existent. They are detached from all dharmas, do not grasp at any dharmas, and do not apprehend any dharmas. One who sees in this way is said to see the Tathāgata.”
Why is this? Sons of good family!
The Tathāgata does not perceive by means of the nature of phenomena; one who perceives that all phenomena are detached from their own nature is called a Tathāgata.
If one can see in this way, it is called right view.
"O sons of good family!
You all should see the Tathāgata in this manner."
"You all should observe as I have taught: observe the Tathāgata in this manner.

Those who observe in this way should know that all dharmas are the Tathāgata; they shall attain the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas, they shall attain the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all dharmas, and they shall attain the non-false mark of all dharmas. They should know that all dharmas are the dharma of the Tathāgata; they should know that all dharmas are the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata; they should know that all dharmas are an inconceivable sphere of activity."
“O sons of good family!
For this reason, I say that all dharmas are the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata, and the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata is a sphere of no-activity. Why is this?
In the sphere of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-gocara*), there is no phenomenon that can be practiced; therefore, it is said that the non-sphere of practice is the sphere of the Tathāgata.
The sphere of all phenomena is itself the non-sphere of practice, and the non-sphere of practice is itself the sphere of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the sphere of activity of all dharmas is non-existent; that which has no sphere of activity is the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata.
All spheres of activity enter the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata, and thus they are not spheres of activity.
Because the Tathāgata has thoroughly realized and attained this Dharma, it is called "the sphere of non-practice" as the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice.
"O sons of good family!

One who can know that all dharmas have no sphere of practice is able to enter the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice; such a person is able to contemplate the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice; such a person is able to seek the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice; and such a person does not even cling to the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice."

Why is this? Because such a person knows that the absence of a place of practice is the Tathāgata’s place of practice, and that being apart from a place of practice is the Tathāgata’s place of practice.

This is because all dharmas are unobtainable, undifferentiable, and beyond craving; thus, what is called "not a place of practice" is the Tathāgata’s place of practice. This is called entering the place of practice of wisdom, for one does not enter into any dharmas.
Why is this? Because all dharmas have no gate; it is through this gate that one enters.
"O sons of good family!
All dharmas have neither entry nor exit; all dharmas are formless. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata has no attainment regarding dharmas.
"What dharma is there that emerges or enters, or is seen or spoken?
O sons of good family! This is called the 'Gate of Entry into All Dharmas.

Because it is characterized by non-entry, all dharmas are without conjunction or dispersion, without bondage or liberation. Since this gate of all dharmas is itself without a gate, this gate is called the 'gate that cannot be exited' and the 'gate that cannot be entered'; it is the 'gate that cannot be returned to' and the 'gate that cannot be described'; it is the gate of ultimate non-arising. By means of this gate of dharmas, one has no knowledge and no vision regarding dharmas."
By means of this Dharma-gate, there is no realization of dharmas and nothing to enter.
Why is this? O sons of good family!
All dharmas have no gate, for a gate cannot be apprehended.
Space is the gate of all dharmas, for its nature has been pure from the very beginning.
Non-interruption is the gate of all dharmas, for there is nothing that can be interrupted.
Boundlessness is a gateway to all dharmas, because limits cannot be apprehended.
Immeasurability is a gateway to all dharmas, because measures cannot be apprehended.
Limitlessness is a gateway to all dharmas, because no limits exist.
“Good sons! If there are good men or good women who are able to enter this Dharma-gate, they will then enter all Dharma-gates, know all Dharma-gates, and expound all Dharma-gates.”
2. Chapter on the Five Aggregates. *The Scripture on Sustaining the World*, Chapter Two on the Five Aggregates, Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sustaining the World:
"Sustaining the World!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain the true mark of all dharmas, wishes to skillfully discern the chapters and phrases of all dharmas, wishes to attain the power of mindfulness, or wishes to transform their body so as to fully attain uninterrupted mindfulness until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should swiftly enter this Dharma-gate and thereby obtain the light of wisdom within this Dharma-gate.
Why is this? Because within these dharmas, one swiftly attains full completion.
Furthermore, World-Upholder!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas diligently cultivate and collect such Dharma-gates, those who enter these gates of skillful means in the Dharma are then able to attain the discernment of the skillful means of the aggregates (skandha), the skillful means of the elements (dhātu), the skillful means of the sense-bases (āyatana), the skillful means of dependently originated phenomena (pratītyasamutpāda), the skillful means of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the skillful means of the five faculties (indriya), the skillful means of the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), the skillful means of mundane and supramundane phenomena, and the skillful means of discerning conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
“Lokadhara! What is meant by the bodhisattva’s skillful means for discerning the five aggregates?

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva correctly contemplates the five aggregates of grasping: namely, the aggregate of ignorance is the five aggregates of grasping; the aggregate of suffering is the five aggregates of grasping; the aggregate of delusion is the five aggregates of grasping; and the aggregate of illness, the aggregate of abscesses, and the aggregate like an arrow piercing the body are the five aggregates of grasping.”
The bodhisattva analytically observes and discerns the aggregate of grasping at form (*rūpôpādānaskandha*).
How does he analytically observe and discern the aggregate of grasping at form?

This aggregate of grasping at form arises from the four great elements; it is conventionally designated as the "aggregate of grasping at form. This aggregate of form has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it exists merely through the combination of the four great elements and is thus conventionally designated as the "aggregate of form."
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) has no agent, nor does it have one who causes it to act; it is without action, without arising, and without emergence—this is called the aggregate of form.

It is merely designated as the "aggregate of form" because it is comprised of the four great elements through the causal conditions of prior karma; yet, in reality, this aggregate is not an aggregate, for like space, the aggregate truly lacks the characteristic of birth.
If one speaks of the aggregate of space, therein no dharma arises; it exists merely as a name, and is therefore called the aggregate of space.

Ordinary beings perceive this non-aggregate as having the characteristic of an aggregate due to their inverted minds. Because of this, they lack the characteristic of reality, yet they greedily cling to "my five aggregates" and "the five aggregates belonging to me," such as "I am the aggregate of form" and "the aggregate of form belongs to me," thus clinging in this manner.

These ordinary worldlings, having become greedily attached to form, rely upon "self" and "what belongs to self" within form; they possess form, experience form, grasp form, cling to form, and depend on form, thereby performing various kinds of evil and unwholesome karmas.

"We should not follow the training of ordinary worldlings; we should diligently cultivate and gather the factors conducive to enlightenment. Now, we must correctly contemplate the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
When a bodhisattva correctly contemplates the aggregate of form, he knows it to be identical to a mass of foam."
How is it known that [the body] is like a mass of foam?
There is no "mass" in a mass of foam;

it arises merely from a combination of conditions, cannot be grasped, and lacks solidity. Within a mass of foam there is no characteristic of a "mass"; this absence of a mass is what constitutes a mass of foam.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is also like this; within the aggregate of form, there is no characteristic of an aggregate.
When the Bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he reflects:
"Ordinary beings cannot correctly contemplate illusory form; they cannot know form as it truly is—impermanent—and they cannot know the characteristics of form as they truly are."
We have entered the Right Path; we should not be greedily attached to the false, nor should we be greedily attached to form (*rūpa*).

Why is this? Form is a characteristic that should not be greedily attached to. Form exists only as a name and lacks any definitive characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); one should contemplate this form as lacking a definitive characteristic. It is called "form" only because it is detached from names.

Furthermore, it is said that form is characterized by affliction and disintegration; the wise penetrate this and know it to be signless (*animitta*). We should skillfully understand and cultivate the means for the signlessness of form, and not be greedily attached to the signs of form.
"If a person is greedily attached to the marks of form, they are greedily attached to form; we should skillfully know how to enter into the marks of form.

When the Bodhisattva contemplates correctly in this way, he observes and discerns form as it truly is: this aggregate of form arises entirely from the conceptualizations and discriminations of ordinary beings.
If a phenomenon arises from conceptualization and discrimination, it is unborn; all conceptualizations and discriminations are not real. Ordinary people rely upon form arising from inversion;

they are bound by form and harmed by form, undergoing the suffering of coming and going. Because of the darkness of ignorance and delusion, they crave form and do not relinquish it, seeing form as permanent and solid. Thus, these ordinary people are bound by form.

Bound by form, they wander through the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, devas, and humans; deeply craving the flavors of form, they fail to contemplate the various faults and evils inherent within it.
"We should not follow the training of ordinary worldlings; rather, we should observe, select, discern, and cultivate the skillful means regarding form (*rūpa*).

When observing, selecting, and discerning form, one sees that the nature of form is like a dream. For example, forms in a dream all arise from recollection, conceptualization, and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); they arise from causes and conditions consisting of what has been previously seen, heard, sensed, and known. Even within a dream, one perceives self and other, and one also sees earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as mountains, rivers, groves, and forests."
The forms and appearances within a dream have no fixed reality; they exist only through the power of recollection and imagination.
The characteristics of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) are likewise: arising from the causal conditions of karma from previous lives, they possess no inherent, determinate nature.
The bodhisattva reflects in this way and does not grasp at form—neither as "I" nor as "mine"—but correctly contemplates form as it truly is:

as impermanent in nature, false, and inverted. Sentient beings, being inverted, greedily cling to and grasp at form, [conceiving] it as "my form," "form belonging to me," "another's form," or "form belonging to another."
When one thus correctly observes and discerns form (*rūpa*), one does not apprehend form, nor does one perceive the intrinsic nature of form, nor does one become attached to the impermanence of form.

At that time, the bodhisattva completely severs all affection, craving, and attachment toward form; they skillfully know the true characteristic of form, skillfully know the characteristic of the equality of form, skillfully know the characteristic of the cessation of form, and skillfully know the characteristic of the path to the cessation of form. They skillfully know that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, and they form this thought:
"This bodily aggregate of form arises entirely from the retribution of karma and from discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); it is comprised of the four great elements."
"This physical aggregate of form is neither self nor another, it belongs to nothing, and has no origin.

Observing the aggregate of form in this way, one does not crave or grasp at internal form, nor does one crave or grasp at external form; one does not crave or grasp at past form, nor future form, nor present form. Thus, one knows that all aggregates of form possess the characteristic of non-arising.
At that time, this bodhisattva neither extinguishes form nor seeks the dharma of extinguishing form.
World-Holders!
This is how a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes and discerns the aggregate of grasping at form.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s observation and selection regarding the appropriation of the aggregates?
The bodhisattva reflects as follows:”

"These painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings all arise from causes and conditions; they belong to the various causes and conditions that enter into the characteristic of feeling.
Within this, there is no feeler; it is merely due to craving and attachment. That which craves and attaches is itself unreal and false, arising from recollection, thought, and discrimination."
When this bodhisattva reflects in this way, he thinks:
"These ordinary worldlings are bound by false sensations and are afflicted by the three types of sensation—namely, painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations."
When these ordinary persons experience pleasure, they are driven by the fetter of craving; because they are driven by the fetter of craving, they are able to give rise to unwholesome karma.
When they experience suffering, they are driven by the fetter of aversion; because they are driven by the fetter of aversion, they give rise to various unwholesome karmas.

If one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one is driven by the fetter of ignorance; because this person is driven by the fetter of ignorance, they are not liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.
"We should not now follow the training of ordinary worldlings; we should correctly contemplate all phenomena. We should contemplate all sensations (*vedanā*) as they truly are.
Thus the Bodhisattva contemplates the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) as it truly is and reflects:

"What is not an aggregate is the aggregate of sensation; it arises from recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination. It is associated with inversion and lacks a feeler; it arises solely from the causal karma of previous lives and the conditions of the present life."
"All sensations are empty of intrinsic nature; within sensation, there is no characteristic of sensation.

Thus, the Bodhisattva contemplates and penetrates the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), seeing it as being like raindrops or bubbles on water: subject to arising and ceasing, they possess no fixed permanence.

The aggregate of sensation is likewise: it arises through a sequence of causes and conditions; belonging to these causes and conditions, it has no moment of abiding; it is false and unreal, arising from the correspondence of recollection and inverted views.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Ordinary worldlings are to be pitied; they are constrained by various sensations (*vedanā*). Because they do not contemplate the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) correctly, they develop attachment when experiencing pleasant sensations, develop attachment when experiencing painful sensations, and also develop attachment when experiencing sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant. Bound by these various sensations, they run to and fro, transmigrating from body to body, fettered by the bonds of affliction, revolving through the five destinies without rest."

These ordinary persons are attached to various feelings; they are constrained by feelings and bound by feelings, not liberated from the aggregate of feeling. They do not perceive an exit from within the aggregate of feeling because they do not know how to correctly contemplate the aggregate of feeling.

Not knowing how to contemplate the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) as it truly is—impermanent—one is bound within the aggregate of feeling by the defilement of desire, failing to know the true nature of the aggregate of feeling.
We should now no longer follow the training of ordinary worldlings, but should instead observe and discern the aggregate of feeling according to reality.

Immediately, he contemplates the aggregate of sensation as it truly is: that the absence of an aggregate is the aggregate of sensation, that the unreal aggregate is the aggregate of sensation, that the inverted aggregate is the aggregate of sensation, and that the non-abiding aggregate is the aggregate of sensation.

At that time, one perceives the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) as it truly is: there is no agent, nor is there any instigator of action; within the aggregate of sensation, one does not perceive the characteristic of the aggregate of sensation.

Observing the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) in this way, one does not see the aggregate of sensation within, nor does one see it without; one does not cling to "I" as sensation, nor does one cling to "another" as sensation; one knows that the aggregate of sensation comes from nowhere and belongs to nothing.

That which can give rise to sensation arises solely from the continuity of the illusory causes and conditions of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), which is designated as such by the name of the retribution of karma from previous lives associated with inversion. One thus perceives the continuous activity of the aggregate of sensation as being illusory.

At that time, one does not accept, does not crave, and does not cling to the aggregate of sensation of the past; one likewise does not accept, does not crave, and does not cling to the aggregate of sensation of the future; and one likewise does not accept, does not crave, and does not cling to the aggregate of sensation of the present.

This person eliminates the fetter of craving within pleasant feelings, eliminates the fetter of aversion within painful feelings, and because they perceive and see the fetter of ignorance within neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, they practice with diligent vigor.

At that time, when a bodhisattva experiences a pleasant feeling, no craving arises in the mind; when experiencing a painful feeling, no aversion arises in the mind; and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, no delusion arises in the mind.
“Lokadhara! Ordinary persons mostly give rise to craving toward pleasant feelings, aversion toward painful feelings, and delusion toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.

Because of this craving, aversion, and delusion, these ordinary persons enter deeply into darkness; they cannot know the aggregate of feeling as it truly is, nor do they understand the characteristics of craving, aversion, and delusion. They are profoundly attached to craving, aversion, and delusion, claiming: ‘This is me,’ ‘this is mine,’ ‘this is this one,’ or ‘that is that one.’”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva correctly contemplates the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) herein, he is not led astray by craving, aversion, or delusion.

If craving, aversion, or delusion arise, he is immediately able to sever them and proceed upon the right path. He exerts diligent effort because he severs the fetters and latent tendencies of craving within pleasant sensations; he exerts diligent effort because he severs the fetters and latent tendencies of aversion within painful sensations; and he exerts diligent effort because he severs the fetters and latent tendencies of delusion within sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant.”

When one knows the characteristics of the three types of feeling as they truly are, then whatever is felt—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one remains detached and unattached to them all.

One is free from the fetter and underlying tendency of craving, free from the fetter and underlying tendency of aversion, and free from the fetter and underlying tendency of delusion; whenever any feelings arise, one is able to know and see them, knowing the aggregate of feeling as it truly is: impermanent.

If one can know in this way, then all desire-taints within the aggregate of feeling will be completely severed; entering the path that severs the desire-taints of the aggregate of feeling, one will not be defiled by any feelings.

When this bodhisattva thus correctly contemplates the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and knows the aggregate of feeling as it truly is—knowing its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation—he then knows the aggregate of feeling as having the characteristic of non-arising; through the characteristic of non-arising, he penetrates the signlessness (*animitta*) of the aggregate of feeling.
“World-Holder!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva observes and discerns the aggregate of sensation in this way.
World-Holder!”
What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation and discernment of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva correctly contemplates the aggregate of perception, they see that the aggregate of perception arises entirely from inversion; it is false, not solid, and not real. From the very beginning it has had no marks of arising, yet through the conjunction of causes and conditions, it arises from the karmic power of previous lives.
He forms this thought:

"The aggregates are not the aggregate of perception; false aggregates are the aggregate of perception; inverted aggregates are the aggregate of perception; within the aggregate of perception, there is no notion of an 'aggregate of perception'."

For example, like a mirage in the month after spring, it is called a "mirage" by way of designation; so too with the aggregate of perception: because it has the characteristic of consciousness, it is called the aggregate of perception.

Ordinary worldlings are bound by false conceptualizations regarding this [body]: they may perceive pleasure, or perceive pain, or perceive neither-pain-nor-pleasure; they may perceive cold or heat; they may perceive male or female; they may perceive birth-and-death within the five destinies; they may perceive conjunction or separation; they may perceive the past, the future, or the present; they may perceive beauty or ugliness; or they may perceive existence or non-existence.
These perceptions of ordinary beings are all inverted and false, dependent upon various causes and conditions, and are merely designated as the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
Within this, whether internal or external, there is no perceiver, for they are bound by the deluded and false perceptions of ordinary beings.

They may perceive desire, or perceive anger, or perceive ignorance, or perceive wives and children; ordinary people rely upon this aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and are attached to what is false. Because of this aggregate of perception, they run to and fro, unable to contemplate the aggregate of perception as it truly is—as being false.

Ordinary worldlings, by means of the notion of self, the notion of others, and the notions of male and female, are bound to the aggregate of perception and cannot attain liberation. They are greedily attached to the aggregate of perception, thinking: "I am the aggregate of perception; the aggregate of perception is mine."
"We should not follow the training of ordinary worldlings.

Thus the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva correctly contemplates the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); within the aggregate of perception, the perception of the aggregate of perception cannot be apprehended, just as within a mirage, the characteristic of a mirage cannot be apprehended.

The Bodhisattva perceives the aggregate of perception as being like a mirage. He does not crave, accept, or cling to the aggregate of perception of the past; he likewise does not crave, accept, or cling to the aggregate of perception of the future; and he does not dwell upon the aggregate of perception of the present, nor does he discriminate between "self" and "other. This is the path that extinguishes the aggregate of perception and feeling; through it, he penetrates the realization that the aggregate of perception is unborn.

One does not perceive a coming or a going of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); it arises solely from the causes of past karma associated with inversion and is bound by present conditions. This aggregate of perception is, in itself, no aggregate; one observes and discerns the aggregate of perception as having nowhere from which it comes and nowhere to which it goes. Thus, one penetrates the non-arising of the aggregate of perception and does not conceptualize its cessation, but rather for the sake of extinguishing all aggregates of perception and feeling (*vedanā*), and because one abides in knowledge and vision according to reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna-darśana*).
"When a bodhisattva contemplates the aggregate of perception as it truly is, they distance themselves from all mental paths of perception and do not abide in any mental path of perception.

They simply abide in the knowledge and vision of the aggregate of perception, and likewise contemplate the aggregate of perception as it truly is. They do not crave or cling to the aggregate of perception, but observe all aggregates of perception as they truly are, knowing as they truly are the arising, cessation, and exhaustion of the aggregate of perception."
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus correctly observes and discerns the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), they become free from the defilement of desire for the aggregate of perception, and are also able to practice the path that severs the defilement of desire for the aggregate of perception.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s observation and discernment of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha)?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) arises from inversion; it exists only through false recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, being merely borrowed and provisional.
At that time, whether the Bodhisattva engages in physical, verbal, or mental activity, they contemplate all as impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
When observing in this way, one forms this thought: "The aggregates are not [inherently existent];

they are the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The aggregate of suffering is the aggregate of formations; the aggregate born of causes and conditions is the aggregate of formations; the aggregate of images is the aggregate of formations. All aggregates of formations neither increase nor decrease, and there is no accumulation."
If there is no agent for bodily action, verbal action, or mental action, the wise do not greedily accept this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Why is this?
These various bodily actions do not exist within the body, nor do they exist outside the body, nor do they exist in between.
The same applies to verbal formations and mental formations: they do not exist within the mind, nor do they exist outside the mind, nor do they exist in between.
Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there is no characteristic of the aggregate of formations.

Why is this? This aggregate of formations arises from various causes and conditions through inversion; it is false and unreal, subsumed under the retribution of prior karma, and furthermore, being bound by causes and conditions, it is capable of performing actions.

All conditioned formations—whether bodily formations, verbal formations, or mental formations—are not true formations; they are formations of non-existence, formations of falsehood, and formations of inversion. Therefore, it is said that what are not aggregates are the aggregate of formations.

Why is this? Because the wise do not determinately grasp the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), such as "this is bodily formation," "this is verbal formation," or "this is mental formation," whether in this place or that place, or internally or externally.

Furthermore, since even the activities of body, speech, and mind cannot be apprehended or described as having any determinate characteristics, how much less can the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) be apprehended or described?
Therefore, it is said that the absence of aggregates is itself the aggregate of formations.

Ordinary beings give rise to inverted perceptions, becoming greedily attached to the activities of body, speech, and mind; they recollect and differentiate these as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and being bound by this aggregate of formations, they run to and fro.

Because these ordinary persons act under the influence of inversion, they give rise to actions of body, speech, and mind; having given rise to them, they become attached to and take refuge in them. Where there are no dharmas, they conceive the notion that dharmas exist; where there are no aggregates, they conceive the notion that aggregates exist.

Because of attachment to inverted practices, one is bound by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and wanders through the five destinies. Constantly following the actions of body, speech, and mind, one is unable to contemplate these bodily, verbal, and mental actions as they truly are; because one cannot contemplate the aggregate of formations as it truly is, one gives rise to various formations through body, speech, and mind.
"Because these ordinary worldlings are attached to inversions, attached to unreal dharmas, and attached to falsehoods, they are frequently called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
“World-Holder!

In this regard, the bodhisattva correctly contemplates that all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) have no fundamental basis; being weak, inferior, and powerless, they exist through the conjunction of various conditions, and may thus be described as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

Within this, there is no truly existent aggregate of formations; that which is without aggregates is the aggregate of formations; that which has been unborn from the very beginning is the aggregate of formations; and that which is without intrinsic nature is the aggregate of formations.

All conditioned phenomena cannot be apprehended at their prior limit, cannot be apprehended at their posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in their middle; they have no time of abiding, for all conditioned phenomena arise and perish from moment to moment.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

When a bodhisattva thus correctly contemplates that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty and unobtainable, lacking any mark of solidity such that not even a hair’s breadth can be found, they form this thought:

‘These ordinary worldlings are bound by non-solid phenomena, bound by the aggregate of formations, and fettered by craving; they give rise to the activities of body, speech, and mind, thinking: “I am the formations,” or “The formations are mine.”’”

Arising from such karma, one is bound by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); not knowing the nature of the aggregate of formations, one enters the dark ignorance of delusion. Within all formations, one conceives the notion of reality; due to this inversion, one greedily clings to and grasps the aggregate of formations.

Because this person is greedily attached to and grasps at the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they may give rise to pleasant formations, painful formations, or formations that are neither painful nor pleasant.

Having given rise to pleasant formations, they obtain a pleasant body; having given rise to painful formations, they obtain a painful body; and having given rise to formations that are neither painful nor pleasant, they obtain a body that is neither painful nor pleasant.

When this person obtains a body of pleasure, they give rise to craving; when they obtain a body of suffering, they give rise to aversion; and when they obtain a body of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, they give rise to delusion.

Because of this craving, aversion, and delusion, they do not perceive the faults and evils of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and are thus unable to purify their actions of body, speech, and mind.
Because this person’s conduct of body, speech, and mind is impure, they fall into the impure paths, namely the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;

or at times they may briefly be born among gods or humans, yet they remain greedily attached to their conduct of body, speech, and mind, and are deeply attached to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should contemplate correctly in this way: 'Now we should not follow the training of ordinary worldlings; we should purify our conduct of body, speech, and mind; we should not be greedily attached to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha); we should contemplate the faults and evils of the aggregate of formations; and we should seek the path that leads out from the aggregate of formations.'"

One who contemplates in this manner is said to be practicing the correct contemplation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as it truly is; they are also said to be correctly contemplating the impermanence of the aggregate of formations.

At that moment, one contemplates all formations as they truly are: the arising of formations, the cessation of formations, and the path leading to the cessation of formations. One does not accept, covet, or cling to formations, nor does one covet or cling to the aggregate of formations.

When observing in this way, one distances oneself from the characteristics of formations (*saṃskāra*) and practices the path of non-practice; that is, one contemplates the emptiness of all formations.

Within all formations, one gives rise to fear and a mind of weary detachment, initiating only pure conduct of body, speech, and mind. This is because one destroys the characteristics of formations and detaches from the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Whatever body this person obtains is entirely pure. Why is this?
Because this person’s bodily karma is pure, verbal karma is pure, and mental karma is pure; their bodily conduct is pure, verbal conduct is pure, and mental conduct is pure.
This person distances themselves from the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and destroys the characteristics of all phenomena and their fundamental basis.

When observing correctly in this manner, they see that the aggregate of formations comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; they find no definitive characteristic of arising in any formations, nor do they find a definitive characteristic of cessation. Thus, they observe that all formations lack the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and that all formations are without arising or ceasing.

"This person contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being without the characteristics of arising and ceasing, thereby giving rise to a mind of weary detachment. They correctly penetrate the characteristics of the origination and cessation of all conditioned phenomena.
Although they realize that all conditioned phenomena are without the characteristic of arising, they skillfully penetrate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena."
Why is this? World-Upholder!
This aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) has no determinate characteristic.

For example, just as with a plantain tree, neither a characteristic of solidity nor a characteristic of non-solidity can be found; so too it is with the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), for neither a characteristic of solidity nor a characteristic of non-solidity can be found.
“World-Upholder!
In this way, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe, discern, and contemplate as they enter into the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
— *Lokadhātupaṭala* (The World-Upholder Sūtra), Fascicle One.
The Scripture on Holding the World, Scroll Two, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
The Second Part of the Second Chapter: The Five Aggregates of the Scripture on Holding the World.
“Holder of the World!
What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s correct observation and discernment of the aggregate of consciousness?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes that what is not an aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness; that the inverted aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness; and that the illusory aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness.”
Why is this? Worldly Sustainer!

This aggregate of consciousness arises from inversion; it is bound by false conditions and originates from prior karma. It is bound by present conditions and belongs to a multitude of causes and conditions. It is empty and non-existent, arising from recollection and conceptualization. Because it is produced from consciousness and possesses that which is cognized, it is called "consciousness."

It arises from recollection, conceptualization, applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*); it exists only as a provisional designation. Because there is that which is cognized, it is conventionally termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

It is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) because it cognizes various objects, because it initiates mental karma, because of its deliberation, because it is a phenomenon produced by multiple conditions, and because it gives rise to manifold forms of reflection.

From that which has cognition, the appearance of cognition emerges; because it demonstrates the activity of the mind (*citta-karma*) and because it encompasses reflection (*manasikāra*), it is designated by the name "aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñāna-skandha*).

It is sometimes called "mind," sometimes called "intellect" (*manas*), and sometimes called "consciousness"; because all these are the differentiation of mental activity (*manas-karma*), they are subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness.
