Because it demonstrates the characteristic of consciousness, the activity of consciousness, and the nature of consciousness, it is designated by the name "aggregate of consciousness."

In this way, that which is not an aggregate is the consciousness-aggregate; it is unproduced, unarisen, and unconditioned. It is merely designated by the name "consciousness-aggregate" because it corresponds with inversion and conditions false consciousness.

Why is this? This aggregate of consciousness arises from a multitude of causes and conditions and lacks intrinsic nature; it arises in successive continuity, arising and ceasing moment by moment. This consciousness, as a condition, does not give rise to the characteristics of an aggregate.

Why is this? Because the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) of this aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) cannot be apprehended, and its characteristic of determination (*niyata-lakṣaṇa*) likewise cannot be apprehended.

Because the characteristic of arising cannot be apprehended, because the characteristic of determination cannot be apprehended, because it is fundamentally non-existent, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because it is not found to be solid or stable, the wise, through correct observation, discernment, and penetration, realize that what is not an aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness.

“Ordinary worldlings give rise to the characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) within what is not the aggregate of consciousness. Bound by false imaginings associated with inverted conceptualization, reflection, and discrimination, they forcibly designate it as the ‘aggregate of consciousness. They become greedily attached to this aggregate of consciousness; relying upon that which is cognized and relying upon the various modes of mental activity manifested by consciousness, they give rise to the aggregate of consciousness.”

This person engages in various forms of discrimination, becoming greedily attached to internal consciousness, greedily attached to external consciousness, greedily attached to both internal and external consciousness, greedily attached to distant consciousness, and greedily attached to proximate consciousness; because of these characteristics of consciousness, they give rise to the aggregate of consciousness through discrimination.

This person, through recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, applies provisional and forced names such as "mind," "intellect," or "consciousness" to what is merely mind, intellect, or consciousness; in this way, they perceive the arising of various mental characteristics.

These ordinary beings are greedily attached to the aggregate of consciousness and are bound by it; because the mind, intellect, and consciousness are conjoined, they give rise to various aggregates of consciousness.

By discriminating false and illusory phenomena, and by means of a single characteristic and a determinate characteristic, they are able to apprehend this as mind, this as intellect, and this as consciousness, and are thus able to discriminate and become attached to them.

Because this person relies upon the aggregate of consciousness and deeply craves it, they also give rise to thoughts of craving and attachment toward the past aggregate of consciousness, they give rise to thoughts of craving and attachment toward the future aggregate of consciousness, and they give rise to thoughts of craving and attachment toward the present aggregate of consciousness.

“Ordinary worldlings, within the dharmas of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, reckon that they have attained the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and are greedily attached to the existence of thought. These people, being greedily attached to the dharmas of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, are bound by the aggregate of consciousness; they prize what they know, and because their mind, intellect, and consciousness are joined in bondage, they run to and fro.”
What is meant is that from this world to the next, and from the next world back to this one, all are bound by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

One is unable to know the aggregate of consciousness as it truly is; the aggregate of consciousness is false, unreal, and associated with inversion. It arises conditioned by the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, yet within it there is no real consciousness.

If one cannot contemplate it thus in reality, one may give rise to wholesome consciousness, unwholesome consciousness, or both wholesome and unwholesome consciousness. Such a person constantly follows the movements of consciousness, not knowing the place where consciousness arises, nor knowing the true nature of consciousness.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva correctly contemplates in this manner, he understands that the aggregate of consciousness arises from false consciousness; that is to say, it is produced by various causes and conditions within the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Because one gives rise to the perception of a phenomenon where no phenomenon exists, one becomes greedily attached to the aggregate of consciousness.”

We should not follow the training of ordinary worldlings; we should, in accordance with reality, correctly observe and discern consciousness, and correctly observe and discern the aggregate of consciousness as it truly is.

When these bodhisattvas contemplate in accordance with reality, they know that the aggregate of consciousness is empty, false, and unreal; from the very beginning it has always been characterized by non-arising. They know that what is not an aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness, that the aggregate of images is the aggregate of consciousness, and that the aggregate of illusions is the aggregate of consciousness.
For example, just as a person conjured by illusion has consciousness that is neither within nor without, nor in between, so too is the nature of consciousness.

Like the illusory nature, which is false and born of conditions, arising from conceptualization and discrimination, it lacks any substantial reality—like a wooden puppet operated by machinery. Consciousness is also like this: it arises from inversion and exists through the combination of false causes and conditions.

When observing in this way, one knows that consciousness is entirely impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self; that the characteristics of consciousness are like an illusion, and that the nature of consciousness is observed to be like an illusion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva forms this thought:

"The world is profoundly deluded and foolish, in that it gives rise to the world from the conceptualization and discrimination of consciousness, uniting with mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*). The three realms are nothing but consciousness; this mind, intellect, and consciousness is also formless and directionless, neither within phenomena nor outside of phenomena."

Because ordinary persons are bound by association with falsehood, they are greedily attached within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to either a self or what belongs to a self. Such a person is greedily attached to the aggregate of consciousness as being internal, greedily attached to it as being external, greedily attached to it as being both internal and external, and greedily attached to it as being "that" or "self. This person prizes this aggregate of consciousness and is bound by it; they experience the flavor of the aggregate of consciousness and describe its characteristics—namely, whether it be mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because they follow the course of these flavors, they greedily accept the aggregate of consciousness. Thus, such a person is bound by consciousness; because of their conjunction with the aggregate of consciousness, they are dragged along by mind, thought, and consciousness.

By the power of the causes and conditions of mind, intellect, and consciousness, this ordinary person is born. If they give rise to an inferior volition, they obtain an inferior body; if they give rise to a superior volition, they obtain a superior body; if they give rise to a middling volition, they obtain a middling body. This person is born according to the power of mind, intellect, and consciousness; relying upon the various sense bases (*āyatana*) and being greedily attached to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), they do not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.

"In this regard, the Bodhisattva correctly contemplates and discerns the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as it truly is. Because he correctly contemplates the aggregate of consciousness as having the characteristic of impermanence (*anitya-lakṣaṇa*), he does not crave, cling to, or dwell upon past consciousness; he knows that what is not an aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness."

Regarding the aggregate of consciousness in future lives, one does not crave it, does not cling to it, and does not dwell upon it, knowing that what is not an aggregate is the aggregate of consciousness.
One does not rely upon the aggregate of consciousness in the present either.
One knows the aggregate of consciousness as it truly is: its characteristic of impermanence; one knows the aggregate of consciousness as it truly is: its characteristic of arising and ceasing.

If one contemplates and correctly observes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) in this manner, it is called the path of correct observation for entering the aggregate of consciousness. That is to say:

knowing consciousness as it truly is, knowing the origin of consciousness as it truly is, knowing the cessation of consciousness as it truly is, and knowing the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is. Such a person, by observing the characteristics of the origin and cessation of the aggregate of consciousness as they truly are, is able to dismantle the aggregate of consciousness and sever all signs. They know the characteristics of the origin and cessation of the aggregate of consciousness, and they also penetrate the characteristics of the origin and cessation of the aggregate of consciousness.

At that time, the Bodhisattva neither gives rise to the aggregate of consciousness nor extinguishes the aggregate of consciousness; since this aggregate of consciousness has been non-arising from the very beginning, when observing in this way, one does not differentiate the characteristic of the extinction of consciousness, but penetrates the characteristic of the non-arising of the aggregate of consciousness.
Why is this? World-Holders!

This aggregate of consciousness is without arising, without marks, and without formation; because the nature of the arising of this aggregate of consciousness is false, it enters into the mark of non-arising.
“Holding the World!

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) never possesses the characteristic of being produced or generated; this characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness arises from various causes and conditions.
Holding the World!”

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the dharma of dependent origination in this way, they see that what is not the aggregates is the consciousness-aggregate; by observing, discerning, believing, understanding, realizing, and penetrating all forms of consciousness, they know them all to be truly as they are.
Because the Bodhisattva knows that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is real, all objects of cognition are thus destroyed.
"World-Holder!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the aggregate of consciousness in this way, he knows that this aggregate of consciousness has no producer, no agent, no originator, no experiencer, and nothing experienced; it arises merely through various conditions and exists because various conditions combine. It is bound by the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, yet from the very beginning it is eternally and ultimately empty."

When observing the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) in this manner, one immediately knows that the aggregate of consciousness has the characteristic of being unconditioned and non-arising; thus, one does not prize it nor cling to it.
"Worldly Sustainer!
In this way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva correctly observes, discerns, and enters the aggregate of consciousness."

If a bodhisattva can thus skillfully enter the five aggregates and can thus skillfully and correctly contemplate the five aggregates, this is called penetrating the entry into the origin, cessation, and path of the five aggregates; they are able to sever all characteristics of the aggregates and truly know the skillful means regarding the five aggregates.

By means of these skillful methods, one does not crave, cling, bind oneself to, or be fettered by the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). One knows form (*rūpa*) as it truly is: its characteristic of impermanence. Thus, if there is any desire or defilement regarding form, the Bodhisattva is able to eliminate and sever it.

Likewise, one knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are; one knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are: their characteristic of impermanence. If there is any desire or defilement within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, the Bodhisattva is able to eliminate and sever it.

Because the bodhisattva eliminates and severs the defilement of desire within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*), they accord with and penetrate the definitive skillful means regarding the five aggregates. When observing in this manner, they are able to know the subtle characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to observe and discern the subtle marks of arising and ceasing within the five aggregates of clinging?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes sentient beings first entering the womb at the stage of the kalala, he sees that as soon as the previous five aggregates cease, there immediately arise another set of five aggregates.”

From that time onward, he contemplates the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); although he first perceives the cessation of consciousness, he also knows that the five aggregates do not possess the characteristic of total annihilation; and although they depend upon the *kalala* stage of embryonic development, he also knows that the five aggregates neither arrive from elsewhere nor are permanent.

Thus one contemplates the characteristic of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) in the very first moment of entering the womb; from the stage of the kalala through birth, and subsequently through growth until the time of death, one contemplates the characteristic of the arising and ceasing of these five aggregates of clinging in every thought-moment, thereby observing and discerning the subtle characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging.

“World-Holder! These subtle marks of arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging are as follows: first, the five aggregates of clinging cease; then, in succession, there is nothing until they reach the womb. At the moment consciousness first unites [with the embryo], the five aggregates immediately undergo arising and ceasing. Based on the kalala stage of the five aggregates of clinging, we conventionally designate it as a ‘person.’”
Why is this so? World-Holder!
Consciousness has no basis upon which it can abide; that which consciousness depends upon is the five aggregates of clinging.
“World-Upholder!
Furthermore, you should know that the subtle marks of arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging among the devas in the formless realm are likewise thus.
World-Upholder!”
Such subtle characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging are beyond the reach of the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas, let alone that of śrāvakas.

Only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, thoroughly know the five aggregates of clinging, from the subtle characteristics of their arising and ceasing at the very moment of entering the womb, up to the moment-to-moment arising and ceasing of all aggregates among the formless heavens; this is what is called "all-encompassing wisdom," the wisdom that transcends all worlds.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and reaches the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom, although such a person thus observes and discerns the subtle characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*)—from the initial entry into the womb up to the formless heavens—they still cannot exhaustively fathom them as the Buddhas know them.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
All Buddha-Tathāgatas possess no wisdom that follows after others; they spontaneously attain all wisdom and skillful means, and thus realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The wisdom of all Buddhas reaches everywhere; the unimpeded wisdom of all Buddhas attains decisive insight into all phenomena and achieves sovereign power over all phenomena.
Why is this? Because they have practiced the profound Dharma for immeasurable, innumerable, thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
“Holder of the World!

All ordinary beings are unable to contemplate the five aggregates of clinging through such skillful means, let alone contemplate the subtle marks of arising and ceasing within the five aggregates of clinging. Why is this?
Ordinary worldlings are unable to know the five aggregates of clinging as they truly are; these worldlings do not know grasping, nor do they know the aggregates of clinging.
"World-Holder! What is meant by 'grasping'?"

The grasping at a self, the grasping at sentient beings, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and rituals, the grasping at the five aggregates, the grasping at the eighteen elements, and the grasping at the twelve links of dependent origination—these are called grasping.

Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, whether internal or external—namely, grasping at desire, grasping at existence, grasping at what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, and grasping at "I" and "mine."

“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! Ordinary people, through ignorance and lack of knowledge and vision, grasp at this as false; they grasp at all phenomena due to inverted causes and conditions. Such persons are bound by grasping: with ignorance as a condition, they grasp at volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); with volitional formations as a condition, they grasp at consciousness (*vijñāna*); with consciousness as a condition, they grasp at name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Sentient beings, being defiled by and attached to the coarse characteristics of name-and-form, take refuge therein.”

What is called the clinging to form, the union with form, and the bondage to form; as well as the grasping of the four formless aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which are distinguished as "name.
"World-Honored One!
If there were no Buddhas, sentient beings would have nothing to know and nothing to see, and would be unable to correctly contemplate the five aggregates of clinging."

The Buddhas appear in the world to destroy sentient beings' reliance on form, to destroy their reliance on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and to destroy the notion of a unified single characteristic.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, thus provide this analytical teaching:

"That which you rely upon and to which you return is called 'form'; this form is merely a combination of the four great elements. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness exist only as names. Because the characteristics of name-and-form are established, they are spoken of as the five aggregates of clinging."
"You sentient beings, do not greedily cling to these five aggregates of clinging, which are neither firm nor solid.
"World-Upholder!
For what reason does the Tathāgata speak of the five aggregates of clinging?"
"World-Holder!
These ordinary persons, born from inversion and entering the net of ignorance, run to and fro; where do they go?
They greedily grasp at the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging and form this thought:"
"Relying upon this, I shall obtain happiness.

With this perception of pleasure, that person greedily clings to the five aggregates; likewise, with the perception of suffering or the perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, they greedily cling to the five aggregates.
The place to which ordinary persons resort and upon which they rely is called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"Holding the World!

From birth until now, ordinary persons have been blind and do not know what these five aggregates are; they do not know from where the five aggregates come, and because they do not know the five aggregates as they truly are, they greedily grasp at them. For this reason, they are called the 'aggregates of grasping' (*upādāna-skandha*)."
In this regard, who is there that experiences?

Herein, no experiencer can be found; it is only because of inverted attachment, false discrimination, and self-binding through the darkness of ignorance and delusion that one grasps at "I" and "mine," and grasps at "this" and "that. Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of sensation is one of the five aggregates, wherein there is no grasper and no fixed characteristic.

Therefore, the wise know that it is not the aggregates themselves that are the five aggregates of clinging; rather, the inverted aggregates are the five aggregates of clinging, and the aggregates of ignorance are the five aggregates of clinging. It is here that ordinary persons are bound, and through craving they take refuge in the five aggregates of clinging.
Because one returns to craving, one does not know what constitutes grasping (*upādāna*) or what constitutes the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).

It is merely due to being attached to the five aggregates as one's refuge that one wanders through birth and death; because of this attachment to the five aggregates, one rushes about through the various realms of existence.
"To what does craving lead?
Craving leads to views, craving leads to hearing, craving leads to perceptions, craving leads to consciousness, craving leads to craving, and craving leads to ignorance."

These ordinary worldlings are bound by the fetters of craving; they greedily cling to the five aggregates of clinging, are shrouded by the hindrances, and enter into the darkness of ignorance, neither knowing nor perceiving where we have now returned through our attachment to desire.
Bound to what?

Because they do not know, they wander through the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; bound by birth and death, they crave and return to the cycle of existence without relinquishing it, failing to sever the five aggregates and unable to know the true nature of the five aggregates as it really is.
Because they do not know things as they truly are, they are afflicted by various forms of suffering and distress, falling into the prison of empty space and remaining ignorant of the way out.

Since these people do not see the path leading out, they undergo birth and death within the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra. Consequently, they are unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; nor can they cross over the perilous paths of immeasurable births and deaths, nor free themselves from the great mass of suffering. Instead, they return once more to suffering, become attached to suffering, and are driven by suffering.
"What is suffering?
It is the five aggregates of clinging; when they arise, it is only suffering that arises; when they cease, it is only suffering that ceases.
Worldly Sustainer! "
For this reason, I teach the Dharma to my disciples.
You, O bhikṣus!
You should correctly contemplate the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), and you should also know, in accordance with reality, that form has the characteristic of impermanence.
"You! If there is any lustful defilement regarding form, you should swiftly abandon it.

You should correctly contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; you should also know, as they truly are, the impermanent nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. If there is any lustful defilement regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, you should swiftly abandon it. By abandoning lustful defilement, the mind attains right liberation."
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

If there are those who understand the meaning of the Dharma I have taught in this way and are able to practice according to these teachings, they shall attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.”

If a person cannot practice according to the teaching, they will be bound by the fetters of form and constrained by the ties of craving; entering the darkness of ignorance, they greedily grasp at the five aggregates. Because this person greedily grasps at the five aggregates, they are unable to escape the perilous path of birth and death.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! For this reason, I say that the world disputes with me, but I do not dispute with the world.
What is meant by ‘the world’?
Those who are greedily attached to the five aggregates of clinging are encompassed by the world; such people crave and take refuge in the five aggregates and are bound by them.
Not knowing the nature of the five aggregates and not knowing their empty characteristic, they contend with me.
Such a person opposes the Buddha’s words and contends with the Buddha; therefore, they fall into great ruin and affliction.

If there is someone—whether during the Buddha’s lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa—who can thus contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as false, empty, and non-existent; as arising from the darkness of inverted ignorance; as deceptive fictions that merely delude ordinary people; and as things that are not the five aggregates yet resemble them—such a person does not contend with the Buddha and does not oppose the Buddha’s words; therefore, they shall attain liberation from the sufferings of hell, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

The Buddhas do not contend with people; they are called Buddhas because they have severed all disputes and litigation. They merely expound the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, saying: ‘You all!’”
"What was previously grasped is entirely inverted; because of the power of inversion, all sentient beings greedily take refuge in the five aggregates and wander through the world.

Once these people have greedily taken refuge in the five aggregates, they give rise to various false views, greedily take refuge in various names and designations, and greedily take refuge in various sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, and afflictions. These people are ravaged by various false views and afflictions, as well as by various sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, and afflictions; there is no one who can act as their savior, their shelter, their refuge, or their destination—only the Buddha can save them."

Because ordinary people possess narrow minds and meager wisdom, they crave the five desires and rely upon the five aggregates which are fraught with many faults; thus, these ordinary people contend and dispute with the one who is their savior, their refuge, their reliance, and the deliverer from all suffering and affliction.

“Holder of the World! Now I raise my hand: if there are those who perceive the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), who perceive the characteristics of the aggregates, or who are greedy for the five aggregates, I do not act as their teacher; such persons are also not my disciples. They have not followed me in leaving the household life, they do not follow my practice, and they do not take refuge in me. These people have entered onto a false path, a path of delusion, grasping at what is unreal. This is perversion; they do not understand the Buddha’s intent, they do not understand that the Buddha spoke of the five aggregates according to what was appropriate, and they do not understand the Buddha’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Such people do not accept the Buddha’s teaching; they should not receive offerings, yet they receive them.”
I do not even permit such a person to leave the household life, much less allow them to receive the offerings of others.

Why is this? Such a person is a follower of the heterodox paths; that is to say, one who gives rise to the marks of the five aggregates and who greedily clings to and takes refuge in the five aggregates.

“Lokadhara! In the future age, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, many who have gone forth within my Dharma will be those who give rise to the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). They will definitively preach the characteristics of the five aggregates, becoming deeply attached to them and entering into false paths of delusion. Although they have gone forth within my Dharma, with the *kāṣāya* robe wrapped around their necks, they will constantly delight in frequenting the homes of laypeople. You should know that such persons are no different from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), yet they will receive much respect and offerings from the multitude through my Dharma.”
“World-Holder!

I say that those who hold such views regarding the five aggregates, who dogmatically assert the five aggregates, and who are greedily attached to the five aggregates, shall not be permitted to receive even a single drop of water from another person.”

Why is this? Because such a person, within my Dharma, does not possess even the patience that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti); they oppose and contradict my Dharma and turn their backs on the noble practice.

“Dhāraṇīdhara! Therefore, in the future evil age, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should make such a great vow: ‘I shall together protect and uphold such profound sūtras of mine, and I shall also preach the Dharma for the sake of severing sentient beings’ views regarding the five aggregates.’”
“World-Upholder!
In this sūtra, I have taught the destruction of all marks of the aggregates (skandha) and the detachment from clinging to the marks of the aggregates.
At that time, many householders and renunciants, upon hearing such sūtras as these, will give rise to disputes and fail to produce the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).”
Within this context, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should give rise to this great vow:

"In the future evil age, we shall bring great benefit to sentient beings who are greedily attached to the five aggregates and hold false views; that is to say, we shall deliver those beings who are greedily attached to the view of the five aggregates, benefiting them with the Dharma through appropriate skillful means."
"Therefore, World-Holder!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to thoroughly know the true mark of all dharmas and also skillfully discern the phrases and chapters of all dharmas; if they wish to obtain the power of mindfulness, and wish to achieve a rebirth endowed with uninterrupted mindfulness, even unto the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should constantly contemplate these five aggregates as having the mark of impermanence, the mark of suffering, the mark of non-self, the mark of falsity, the mark of lack of solidity, the mark of ultimate emptiness, and the mark of being unborn from the very beginning."

"When one constantly practices right contemplation, all desire-taints within the five aggregates of clinging are able to be severed and abandoned, and one also attains skillful means regarding such profound dharmas as these.
World-Holder!

In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahāmatiśailarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
"World-Upholder!

This Great Mind Mountain King Buddha has a community of eighty billion nayutas of śrāvakas, all of whom are arhats whose outflows are exhausted, as well as eighty billion nayutas of those on the stage of training who are non-returners."
That is to say, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbered forty billion nayutas.
The lifespan of that Great-Mind Mountain-King Buddha was eighty thousand years.
"Sustainer of the World!
At that time, there was a king named Guṇavardhana. This King Guṇavardhana possessed twenty thousand great cities, which were fully prosperous and joyful, and filled with people.

Each city had sevenfold walls, twelve yojanas in length and breadth, composed of the four precious substances. They were surrounded by sevenfold moats, each equipped with railings and seven rows of trees, all covered above by nets of various jewels.
The city walls, moats, trees, and the nets above were all composed of the four treasures—gold, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, and agate.
Each great city had five hundred gardens, all of which were filled with trees bearing garments made of the seven treasures.
In each of these groves there were five hundred jeweled ponds, all filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
"Holding the World!
This King De-yi had eighty thousand court ladies; his principal consort had two sons:
The first was named Amitamati and the second was named Amitabala.
World-Upholder!

These two princes were each sixteen years of age; in their dreams they saw the Buddha, whose exquisite and peerless form was like a Jāmbūnada-golden banner. Seeing him, they were filled with great joy, and upon waking, each spoke a verse. One of them said:
"I have now seen in a dream the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, Golden-hued and adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings, Having accomplished immeasurable merits;
Upon seeing him, my heart attained great joy."
The second person said:
“In my dream I saw the Buddha, as radiant as the sun, Elegant, exquisite, and the most supreme of beings;
Like Sumeru, the king of all mountains, Majestic, lofty, and prominent, bringing joy to behold.”
"Holder of the World!
At that moment, the two sons, Immeasurable Mind and Immeasurable Power, went to their parents and explained these matters in detail, saying to them:
'Now, both of us have seen the Buddha in a dream; we only pray that our parents will grant us permission to go together to the place where the Buddha is.'"

The Buddha has long been in the world, yet we were negligent and failed to perceive him; we have sunk into the mire of the five desires, bound by the fetters of form, and bound by the fetters of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Because we were living at home and were negligent, we were unable to see the Buddha.
"World-Upholder!
After these two princes had spoken these words to their parents, they immediately went to the presence of the Buddha Great-Intention Mountain King."
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for three months of offerings of the four requisites—robes, food, bedding, and medicine.

He adorned a pleasure grove where King Guṇavardhana used to roam on the outskirts of the great city, hanging silk banners and canopies and covering the ground with precious flowers; he then offered it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, requesting them to dwell therein.

During the three months, those two princes provided all manner of musical instruments and articles of enjoyment as offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha; having completed their offerings, they both went forth into homelessness within the Buddha’s Dharma.
“Holder of the World!

The Buddha Great Intent Mountain King, knowing the profound aspirations in the hearts of these two princes, extensively expounded for them this *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Expedient Means Concerning the Five Aggregates, Twelve Bases, and Eighteen Elements*. For forty thousand years, he never slept; he always ate until his belly was full, nor did he lie down to rest, whether sitting or walking in meditation.”

Furthermore, during those forty thousand years, he did not think of anything else, but focused solely on the false and empty nature of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). He understood that these five aggregates arise from inversion and thoroughly penetrated their characteristics. Throughout his entire life, he constantly practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was reborn in Jambudvīpa into the family of a great lay devotee (*mahāśrāvaka*).
When he reached the age of sixteen, he again saw the Buddha in a dream, who preached for him the *Pañcaskandha-aṣṭādaśadhātu-bodhisattva-upāya-sūtra*.
Having heard this Dharma, he immediately felt alarm and dread; for ten thousand years thereafter, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) within the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, through skillful means, he deeply contemplated the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra on the Skillful Means of the Bodhisattvas* regarding the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having completed their full lifespans, they were reborn in the family of a prominent Brahmin in Jambudvīpa.

During the final millennium of the Dharma of Mahāmati Mountain King Buddha, those two, due to their past causes and conditions, again attained renunciation. Their learning was vast and their wisdom was like the ocean; they were also skilled in observing and discerning the nature of these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and entering into the Dharma, understanding it as it truly is. Within that world, they taught and transformed twenty thousand people and two billion devas toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Holder of the World!

From this time forward, these two bodhisattvas will remain of one mind throughout all their successive lives, together encountering ten billion nayutas of buddhas, after which they shall attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.”
Having attained the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), he further encountered one billion nayutas of Buddhas, after which he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These two individuals became Buddhas consecutively within the same kalpa:
the first was named Immeasurable Sound (Amitaghoṣa), and the second was named Immeasurable Light (Amitābha).
“World-Upholder!

Therefore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should diligently practice and cultivate these aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the characteristics of true knowledge and vision regarding other conditioned phenomena, within this pure and undefiled dharma.”

Chapter Three: The Eighteen Natures “Holding the World! What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who skillfully knows the eighteen natures? 1. The nature of the eye; 2. The nature of form; 3. The nature of eye-consciousness; 4. The nature of contact; 5. The nature of feeling; 6. The nature of craving; 7. The nature of the ear; 8. The nature of sound; 9. The nature of ear-consciousness; 10. The nature of contact; 11. The nature of feeling; 12. The nature of craving; 13. The nature of the nose; 14. The nature of odor; 15. The nature of nose-consciousness; 16. The nature of contact; 17. The nature of feeling; 18. The nature of craving; 19. The nature of the tongue; 20. The nature of taste; 21. The nature of tongue-consciousness;

22. The nature of contact; 23. The nature of feeling; 24. The nature of craving; 25. The nature of the body; 26. The nature of touch; 27. The nature of body-consciousness; 28. The nature of contact; 29. The nature of feeling; 30. The nature of craving; 31. The nature of the mind; 32. The nature of mental phenomena; 33. The nature of mind-consciousness; 34. The nature of contact; 35. The nature of feeling; 36. The nature of craving.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully and correctly contemplates the eighteen natures (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), forming this thought:

"The nature of the eye cannot be apprehended within the nature of the eye; this nature of the eye is without self and without what belongs to a self. It is impermanent, lacking solidity, and empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). Because the nature of the eye cannot be apprehended within the nature of the eye, the nature of the eye is illusory and non-existent, arising from conceptualization and discrimination. The nature of the eye has no determinate characteristic; the nature of space is the nature of the eye."
Just as space has no determinate characteristic because it lacks a fundamental basis, so too is the nature of the eye: it has no determinate characteristic and likewise lacks a fundamental basis.
Why is this? Because within the nature of the eye, no substantial entity can be found.

The nature of the eye has no location and no direction; it is not internal, not external, and not in between. The nature of the eye has no determinate characteristic, because it is without any substantial reality.
The nature of the eye cannot be apprehended, for it arises from a multitude of causes and conditions.

The nature of the eye does not belong to the past, the future, or the present; the nature of the eye and the characteristics of the eye cannot be apprehended. The nature of the eye exists merely as the retribution of prior karma, and because it is contingent upon present conditions, it is conventionally designated by the name "nature of the eye."

The nature of the eye is itself the absence of nature; within the nature of the eye, the nature of the eye cannot be apprehended, for it is merely designated as the "nature of the eye" because it is the sphere of activity of consciousness.
"If the eye-faculty is pure, the visible form is within range, and the mind-faculty is engaged—through the conjunction of these three causal conditions, it is termed the 'nature of the eye.

Within this nature of the eye, there is no definitive characteristic of the nature of the eye; the wise person penetrates that the absence of a nature of the eye is the very nature of the nature of the eye."
“World-Holder!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus observe and discern the nature of the eye, they will penetrate the fact that the nature of form is the nature of non-existence.”

Why is this? Within the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*), the nature of form cannot be apprehended; this nature of form is neither conjoined nor dispersed. Because form has no determinate characteristic, it is designated by the name "nature of form."
Form has no fundamental basis and is without discrimination; how much more so is this true of the nature of form?
The nature of form likewise has no fundamental basis; it is neither within form, nor without form, nor in between, being merely a product of recollection, thought, and discrimination.

When form is within the range of visibility and the faculty of the eye is pure, one perceives present forms through association with the mental consciousness; therefore, it is conventionally designated as "the nature of form.
It is like the reflection of a face in a mirror: if the mirror is bright and clean, the appearance of form arises, yet the form within the mirror has no fixed reality.

Just as there is no person within a mirror yet its forms and images are seen—merely because there is a mirror externally and internal forms and characteristics arise—so too, the nature of the eye is pure, and the objects of perception appear when they are situated within the range of visibility.

Just as the images in a mirror are numerically designated by the nature of form (*rūpa*), yet form has no intrinsic nature and no substantial characteristic, and lacks a determinate nature—this is what is called the nature of form. Because all characteristics of form are without self, they are numerically designated by the nature of form; it is according to what sentient beings know that they are spoken of as the nature of form.
"If a bodhisattva knows this nature of form, they know that the nature of form is the nature of non-nature, the nature of non-arising, and the nature of non-activity."

Why is this? This nature of form does not belong to the past, does not belong to the future, and does not belong to the present; it demonstrates the nature of non-existence, demonstrates the nature of falsity, and demonstrates the nature of conventional designation—this is called the nature of form.
To thus observe and discern the nature of form is for the bodhisattva to correctly observe and discern the nature of eye-consciousness.

That is to say: within eye-consciousness there is no eye-consciousness; the nature of eye-consciousness has no permanence; the nature of eye-consciousness has no root and no determinate dharma; the nature of eye-consciousness is not demonstrable.

This nature of eye-consciousness is neither joined nor dispersed, and it has no fundamental basis; it arises solely through the causal conditions of prior karma, belongs to present conditions, and is designated as "eye-consciousness" because it is bound to the condition of form. It is designated as "eye-consciousness" in accordance with the inverted minds of ordinary worldlings; however, for the noble ones who have attained thorough penetration, the nature of eye-consciousness is precisely non-nature.

Why is this? Because the nature of visual consciousness is not fixed; it arises from a multitude of causes and conditions and belongs to those causes and conditions, and for this reason it is conventionally termed the "nature of visual consciousness.
The sphere where consciousness operates is the nature of visual consciousness, and this consciousness is not fixed.

It is said that there is no determinate characteristic because there is no arising, because it demonstrates the false and illusory, because it can differentiate the characteristics of form, and because it can demonstrate conditions.

This "nature of eye-consciousness" is taught according to what sentient beings know; the Tathāgata uses skillful means to differentiate it in order to destroy the notion of a unified single characteristic.

By explaining these eighteen natures, it is shown that consciousness has no fixed characteristics; rather, it is because the eye is pure and can cognize the characteristics of forms, and through the conjunction of these two factors, that "eye-consciousness-nature" is spoken of. It is to demonstrate the true nature of eye-consciousness that "eye-consciousness-nature" is spoken of.

The nature of visual consciousness indicates the sphere of activity of the eye; that which can cognize form is visual consciousness, and its nature is precisely the teaching of the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Why is this?

Because within the nature of visual consciousness, the wise cannot find the characteristics of the nature of visual consciousness, nor can they find the fundamental basis of the nature of visual consciousness within that very nature.

Why is this so? Because there is no fixed nature that constitutes the nature of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The nature of eye-consciousness is spoken of by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). This "nature" that is spoken of is precisely the meaning of non-apprehension. That which has the capacity for seeing is eye-consciousness; it is the arising of mental activity (*manaskarma*) that constitutes the characteristic of eye-consciousness, and therefore it is called eye-consciousness.

"The nature of the eye, the nature of forms, and the nature of eye-consciousness—by means of these natures as gateways, one speaks of the conjunction of the three factors. Because this serves to know the characteristics of all conditions, it is precisely the meaning of being detached from all natures."
What are called the nature of the eye, the nature of form, and the nature of eye-consciousness—by enumerating such categories, one enables sentient beings to enter the path of reality.

Yet herein, there is truly no nature of the eye, no nature of form, and no nature of eye-consciousness. The Tathāgatas speak of knowing and seeing the characteristics of these natures; it is through skillful means that they analytically distinguish and speak of these various natures.
If a person thoroughly penetrates these skillful means regarding the various natures, they will know that the three natures are without nature.
Why is this? Because within the various natures there is no characteristic of nature, and because within the various natures no characteristic can be apprehended.

The nature of the ear, the nature of sound, and the nature of ear-consciousness; the nature of the nose, the nature of fragrance, and the nature of nose-consciousness; the nature of the tongue, the nature of flavor, and the nature of tongue-consciousness; the nature of the body, the nature of tangibles, and the nature of body-consciousness—all are likewise thus.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s discernment of the nature of the mind?
The bodhisattva forms this thought:”

"The nature of mind has no fixed determination because its fundamental basis does not exist; within the nature of mind there is no nature of mind, and this lack of a fixed nature is itself the nature of mind.
It is like various seeds sown in the great earth: through the moisture of water, the warmth of the sun, and the movement of the wind, they gradually sprout.

The sprout does not emerge from the seed, nor does the seed unite with the sprout; when the sprout arises, the seed perishes. The seed is not separate from the sprout, the sprout is not separate from the seed, yet within the sprout there is no seed.

The nature of mind (*manas*) is also like this: because it can give rise to mental karma and manifests the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is called the "nature of mind," just as a seed is designated by the name "sprout.
Apart from the nature of mind, there is no mind; the nature of mind cannot itself know the mind. It is only by way of conventional designation that it is spoken of as the "nature of mind."

This nature of mind does not exist within the mind, nor does it exist outside the mind, nor does it exist in between; it arises solely due to the causal conditions of prior karma. Because consciousness is the activity of the mind, because it cognizes its objects, because various natures and names combine, and because it arises dependently in the present, it is designated by the name "nature of mind. This is precisely the characteristic of the indeterminate mental activity, and it is the characteristic of the conjunction of manifold conditions.

It is also said that the nature of the mind arises from a combination of conditions; however, according to what sentient beings perceive, in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no such thing as the nature of the mind. Why?
Because it is fundamentally non-existent; this nature of the mind is non-arising, for arising itself is non-existent.
The nature of mind is a conventional expression; in the ultimate sense, the nature of mind is definitively non-existent, for it cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present.
The wise person penetrates the realization that the absence of intrinsic nature is itself the nature of mind.

“Bodhisattvas contemplate and discern the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): the absence of nature is the nature of phenomena; the nature of phenomena has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for an intrinsic nature is unapprehendable. The absence of determinate nature is the nature of phenomena, because the root of the nature of phenomena is unapprehendable and determinate entities are likewise unapprehendable.”

It is only because there are objects of knowledge arising from the false fetters and inverted views of sentient beings that one speaks of "dharma-nature"; it is because one wishes to lead sentient beings into the state of non-nature that this dharma-nature is taught.

Why is this? Within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is no characteristic of a nature of phenomena; this nature of phenomena arises from a multitude of conditions. Phenomena arising from a multitude of conditions lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Within all causes and conditions, there is no intrinsic nature; all causes and conditions arise in succession due to the conjunction of a multitude of conditions and through inversion.

The Tathāgata, wishing here to transform sentient beings, speaks of this dharma-nature; by means of conventional language, he demonstrates the dharma of non-nature. This dharma-nature is neither within, nor without, nor in between. It is intended only to cause sentient beings to know and see wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, for it is through the dharma-nature that one is taught to be free from the characteristics of all dharmas and to perceive them as ultimately empty in nature.
It is said that ultimate emptiness is itself the dharma-nature.
Why is this? That which is non-existent is the dharma-nature; within the dharma-nature, there is no determinate characteristic of existence.
For example, although space has no determinate characteristic, it is conventionally designated as "space"; likewise, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) also has no determinate characteristic.
Because it deconstructs the characteristics of phenomena, it is called the "nature of phenomena," yet this nature of phenomena is itself the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).

Why is this? This dharmatā does not exist in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present; it merely belongs to the various conditions, and because it accords with those conditions, it is conventionally designated as "dharmatā" and spoken of as "dharmatā," just as it is known by sentient beings.

The wise realize that the absence of intrinsic nature is the dharma-nature (dharmatā). This dharma-nature is neither conjoined nor dispersed; within the dharma-nature there is no characteristic of dharma-nature, neither more nor less. It is for the sake of demonstrating the skillful means regarding this nature that the dharma-nature is designated by the name "nature."

"If a practitioner truly penetrates the characteristics of this dharma-nature, they will know and see its lack of intrinsic nature. Within the dharma-nature of these three realms, there is no characteristic of discrimination; yet because of the conjunction of various causes and conditions and because of the conceptualization of all dharmas, one speaks of 'dharma-nature. This indicates that the absence of any fixed nature is itself the dharma-nature."
The wise do not perceive the dharma-nature by means of the characteristics of the dharma-nature; for the dharma-nature is characterized by non-arising.
Why is this? Because within the dharma-nature there are no characteristics.

The wise person penetrates that signlessness is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Within the nature of phenomena, there are no marks of conceptual differentiation; because it is signless and without conceptual differentiation, it is called the nature of phenomena.

Within the nature of phenomena, there is no place of abiding; it has no location, no arising, no staying, and no support. This is because the nature of phenomena is from the very beginning unborn, and thus this nature of phenomena has no producer.
Why is this? Because within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) there is no intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, the nature of phenomena does not exist by way of conjunction; it is without conjunction and without dispersion, without activity and without determination—this is called the nature of phenomena.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate and discern the nature of dharmas in this way, it is what is called "the absence of intrinsic nature" as the dharma-nature.
"World-Holder!
What is meant by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplating and discerning the nature of mental consciousness?"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:

"The nature of non-arising is the nature of mental consciousness; the nature of indeterminacy is the nature of mental consciousness. The nature of mental consciousness has no root and possesses no fixed dharma; by means of the nature of mental consciousness, it demonstrates the characteristic of non-nature."

Why is this? Within the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the nature of mental consciousness cannot be apprehended; this nature of mental consciousness is false and non-existent. It is associated with inversion, taking the mind (*manas*) as its precursor, and it is called "mental consciousness" because it cognizes all phenomena. Because it follows the conduct of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the nature of mental consciousness is thus described.
The noble ones observe and know that it is not the nature of consciousness, but rather the nature of consciousness is that which is false and non-existent.

It is only because of the demonstration of the law of dependent origination, because the mind is primary, and because consciousness arises from the conjunction of various conditions, that it is called the nature of mental consciousness; it is spoken of in this way in accordance with what sentient beings understand.

"The wise know that what is not the nature of consciousness is the nature of mental consciousness; it arises from a multitude of causes and conditions and originates from recollection, thought, and discrimination. It possesses no inherent nature or characteristics, which is precisely the meaning of the absence of inherent nature and characteristics within the ultimate truth."

Within the conventional truth, for the sake of guiding sentient beings, this is called the nature of mental consciousness; it is intended to lead sentient beings to know that the nature of mental consciousness is "no-nature. However, because one destroys and detaches from all natures by means of minor dharmas, it is called the nature of mental consciousness.

Why is this? Because when the sages seek it, it cannot be found. The nature of mental consciousness does not exist within mental consciousness, nor does it exist outside of mental consciousness, nor does it exist in between. The wise person penetrates that the non-conjunction of these natures is what constitutes mental consciousness. Mental consciousness does not know the nature of the mind, and the nature of the mind does not know mental consciousness; they merely arise from a multitude of causes and conditions. They originate from inversion, with the mind as the primary factor. Because they know the conjunction of two things among all conditions, because they cling to the false, because they arise from vitarka and vicāra, and because they manifest the characteristics of consciousness to sentient beings, they are called the "nature of mental consciousness."

This mental consciousness does not abide in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, and has no place of dwelling. From the very beginning, it is characterized by non-arising.
Within the mental consciousness, there is no dharma of fundamental meditative concentration. Why is this?

Because the nature and characteristics of this mental consciousness are themselves non-dual, that is, they are signless (*animitta*). These characteristics do not exist by virtue of dualistic characteristics; the nature of being unindicatable is the very nature of mental consciousness.

"The wise person penetrates the nature of mental consciousness; this nature of mental consciousness does not abide within any phenomena, has no location and no direction, and neither joins with nor disperses from phenomena."

The Sage penetrates the mark of non-arising, which is the nature of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); this nature of the mental consciousness neither comes nor goes and has no object-condition (*ālambana*). Why is this?
Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the nature of the mental consciousness is without object-condition; it cannot be apprehended and cannot be demonstrated.

The wise person penetrates the nature of mental consciousness; this nature of mental consciousness is non-active, because an agent cannot be found. This nature of mental consciousness is unarisen, because the characteristic of arising does not exist.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates and discerns the nature of mental consciousness in this way.
When bodhisattvas practice such contemplation, they discern that the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are all of a nature that is unarisen and non-existent.”
What is meant by contemplation?
It is said that within the realm of desire there is no realm of desire; within the realm of form there is no realm of form; and within the formless realm there is no formless realm.

By means of the elements, they demonstrate the dharma of non-elements: for those who grasp the characteristics of the desire realm, they demonstrate this as the desire realm; for those who grasp the characteristics of the form realm, they demonstrate this as the form realm; and for those who grasp the characteristics of the formless realm, they demonstrate this as the formless realm.

By means of provisional designations regarding the realms (*dhātu*), one speaks of "no-realms," as is known by the wise: the realm of non-existence is itself the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The wise do not apprehend a desire realm, a form realm, or a formless realm; these three realms are all without root and possess no fixed nature, arising from a multitude of conditions. Therefore, the wise know and see that "no-realms" is the three realms.
Within this, there is no characteristic of a realm; these three realms are all false and joined with inverted practices. Why is this?
Because the wise do not apprehend the three realms, nor do they speak of the three realms—whether past, future, or present.

The noble ones and sages thoroughly understand that these three realms are illusory and non-existent, devoid of intrinsic nature and detached from all phenomena; they arise solely from inversion. To sever the inversions of sentient beings and to bring about their knowledge and vision of the three realms, the Tathāgata has analytically explained the characteristics of the three realms. Desiring to lead sentient beings to understand the meaning of "no-realm," he taught that the three realms do not exist by way of intrinsic nature or characteristics. The wise know and see that the characteristics of the three realms are, in fact, the characteristics of no-realm.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this way, he perceives that the nature of sentient beings and the nature of the self are identical to the nature of empty space, the nature of non-existence, and the nature of non-arising.”

Why is this? Because the nature of sentient beings, the nature of the self, and the nature of space are without distinction or difference; all such natures emerge from emptiness. They are designated as "natures" only because they arise from various conditions; within them, there is definitively no characteristic of a nature.
Why is this? Because within empty space there is no fixed nature or characteristic; all these natures and characteristics enter into empty space, which is the meaning of non-existence.

For example, as empty space has no nature, so too these dharmas are ultimately free from characteristics and possess no characteristics of existence; all natures are likewise free from the characteristics of nature. Within all natures there are no characteristics of nature; these characteristics of nature are not within, not without, and not in between.
Within nature there is no nature; nature does not encompass nature; nature does not rely upon nature; all natures have nothing upon which they rely; all natures are unarisen.

The wise, among all natures, do not find a nature that arises, do not find a nature that ceases, and do not find a nature that abides; all natures are neither born, nor produced, nor abiding, being unobtainable from the very beginning.

The wise do not crave or cling to the provisional names of all natures; they neither accept nor dwell upon them. Therefore, the wise penetrate and realize that all natures possess the characteristic of non-arising.

If there is the characteristic of non-arising, then there is no cessation; within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all natures (*bhāva*) are unobtainable. It is only according to conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) that one analytically speaks of various natures; in the ultimate truth, one does not speak of various natures. The wise, through knowledge and vision, penetrate all natures as being identical to the ultimate truth.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva thus contemplates, discerns, and penetrates the eighteen natures, as well as the nature of sentient beings in the three realms, the nature of the self, and the nature of space.”

When the bodhisattvas thus contemplate, discern, and penetrate [reality], they do not apprehend an intrinsic nature nor perceive an intrinsic nature; yet they also penetrate the fact that all natures are merely conventional designations. They also have faith and understanding that the intrinsic nature of all bases (āyatana) is the absence of intrinsic nature, and they also know how to differentiate among these natures.

Based on worldly convention, one analytically explains the various natures so that all natures may enter into the ultimate truth; one also skillfully masters the expedient means of the absence of nature, and furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, one analytically explains the various natures and causes sentient beings to dwell well within those natures.

Using worldly language, he teaches the dharma of non-substantiality to sentient beings; nor does he demonstrate the various natures through dualistic characteristics. Although he knows that all natures are non-dual, he also employs skillful means to explain that these natures arise from causes and conditions.

Although they guide sentient beings by means of worldly discourse, they demonstrate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to them; although they are skilled in discerning all natures (*svabhāva*), they have faith, understanding, and thorough penetration into the fact that all natures are non-existent.
Why is this? World-Holder!
Because the Tathāgata, by virtue of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), finds nothing to be apprehended in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor does he apprehend the characteristics of any natures.
“Dharaṇīśvara!
I have attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi without severing or destroying any natures (dharmas). Why is this?

In the ultimate sense, there are no natures; all natures are non-existent and lack any fixed determination. All natures are identical to space, all natures enter into space, and all natures are devoid of the characteristic of arising. It is in this manner that the Tathāgata thoroughly penetrates all natures.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
The Tathāgata does not speak of the characteristics of various natures, nor does he speak of the power and influence of various dharmas. Why is this?
If dharmas are non-existent, one should not further speak of the nature and characteristics of non-existence.
Worldly Sustainer!
Although the Tathāgata also speaks of the nature and characteristics of non-existence, herein there is truly no nature or characteristic being spoken of.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
This is called the skillful discernment of all natures (*dhātu*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this skillful discernment, they are able to know that all natures are mere conventional designations; they are able to know the characteristics of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are able to know the characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and they are able to know the certainty of all natures. They are able to know worldly truth, they are able to discern various characteristics, they are able to know what is appropriate to circumstances, they are able to know the conjunction of characteristics, they are able to know the intent of characteristics, they are able to know the entry-points of characteristics, they are able to discern characteristics, they are able to know that all characteristics are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and they are able to cause all natures to be identical to the nature of space, without making any distinctions among those natures.”
Within all natures, no distinction is found nor is any distinction spoken of; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, one skillfully explains the destruction of all natures.
"World-Holder!
It is like a skilled illusionist who can manifest various illusory things to sentient beings, causing them to know the various characteristics of illusions."

If there are acquaintances or close friends, one tells them that these things are illusions; one explains that illusory phenomena are real facts, yet they are illusory and false, pointing this out to deluded sentient beings so that those with wisdom may know them to be illusions.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

The nature of the world is like an illusion. When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into this illusory dharma, they know that the world is of an illusory nature and that the activities of the world are like an illusion. By means of their power of skillful means, these people demonstrate to sentient beings that the world is like an illusion.”
If there are those who know this world as it truly is, for them one explains that the world is false and like an illusion.

If there are those with profound wisdom and sharp faculties, they can understand it by themselves without being instructed; they know that all phenomena are empty, like illusions, without reality and without foundation. They know that all phenomena deceive ordinary people, and that all phenomena are bound within the midst of false conditions.
“World-Holder!

Therefore, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to enter into such skillful means regarding all natures (*dharmatā*), they should remain unstained by and non-attached to such profound sūtras. They should explain the characteristics of the knowledge and vision of all natures; they should explain that all natures are without words and without synthesis; they should also explain the skillful means and wisdom regarding natures; they should also explain the purport of what is produced through causes and conditions; and they should also explain the true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.”

Regarding what are called the mundane and the supramundane, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the fettered and the unfettered; skillfully knowing the purport of expedient means; explaining the ultimate meaning and the conventional meaning; the definitive sutras and the non-definitive sutras—through various causes and conditions for such explanations—one should apply oneself with diligent vigor toward these profound sutras.

Chapter Four: The Twelve Bases (*Dvādaśāyatana*) The Buddha told Dharaṇīṃdhara:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who skillfully knows the twelve bases?”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva correctly contemplates and discerns the twelve bases (āyatana), he reflects:
"Within the eye, the eye-base is unapprehendable; within the eye, the eye-base has no fixed existence; furthermore, the root of the eye-base is unapprehendable."

Why is this? The eye-base arises from a multitude of conditions and originates from inversion; because it takes form as its object, it is bound to form, and exists through the conjunction of these two factors.

Because of form there is the eye-base; because of form the eye-base is spoken of. Since these two phenomena depend upon one another, they are called "eye and form. Regarding what is called "eye and form":

form is the "door of entry" for the eye because it serves as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); the eye is the "door of entry" for form because it serves as the faculty of seeing. Therefore, they are called "bases" (*āyatana*).

The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is spoken of because of its dependence on form; the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) is spoken of because it is seen by the eye. This is spoken of only according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); in reality, the eye does not depend on form, nor does form depend on the eye; the eye does not depend on the eye, nor does form depend on form. Rather, they arise from a multitude of conditions: because form acts as a condition, it is called the eye-base;
furthermore, because it arises from a multitude of causes and conditions and is the characteristic perceived and known by the eye, it is called the form-base.
How is it taught?

It is taught in accordance with conventional, inverted phenomena; within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) cannot be found, nor can the sense-base of form (*rūpa-āyatana*) be found.
When the wise seek among the sense bases (āyatana), they do not perceive any truly existent bases.
It is only because ordinary people are associated with inverted views that they speak of these two characteristics, saying, "this is the eye-base" and "this is the form-base."

These are the sense-base of the eye and these are the sense-base of form; this is shown to be the entrance into falsehood, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to know the true reality of all phenomena as it truly is. Thus he says that all these sense-bases arise from various causes and conditions and are associated with inverted formations; herein, the true reality of the sense-bases cannot be apprehended.

Why is this? Whether it be the eye-base or the form-base, they do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between. The eye-base and the form-base are neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present; yet, because one perceives forms through present causes and conditions, one speaks of the "eye-base."

Just as ordinary people act, the wise penetrate that all the sense bases (*āyatana*) are entirely false and non-existent, arising from conceptualization, inversion, and discrimination. They know and see that what is not a sense base is a sense base; they do not speak of an intrinsic nature of the sense bases, for the sense bases have no fixed characteristics and are spoken of only because they arise through a multitude of causes and conditions.

“The Tathāgata has spoken of the characteristics of the knowledge and vision of these sense-bases (*āyatana*). That is to say, these sense-bases are false and non-existent; they belong to the functioning of dependent origination associated with inversion. Among these sense-bases, there is no agent and no instigator. The eye-base does not know nor discern the form-base, and the form-base likewise does not know nor discern the eye-base; both are devoid of characteristics.”

If phenomena are devoid of characteristics, they cannot be conceptually distinguished within this state as having the characteristic of "entry. All arise from causes and conditions; as ordinary beings perceive through inversion, so do the noble ones penetrate them: these are the eye-base and the form-base, which are without arising or ceasing, and possess the characteristic of neither coming nor going. The eye does not know the eye, nor does the eye discriminate the eye; form does not know form, nor does form discriminate form.
Why is this? Because both are empty and both are detached.

The eye does not know the nature of the eye, nor does form know the nature of form; both eye and form are without nature and are non-existent dharmas. Within this, there is not a single determinate characteristic.
The eye does not create itself, nor does the eye know itself; form does not create itself, nor does form know itself; for both are devoid of intrinsic existence.

The eye does not form the thought, "I am the eye," nor does form form the thought, "I am form. The nature of the eye and form is like the nature of an illusion; it is only through false and provisional designations that they are called "eye" and "form."

In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas discern and examine the sense base of the eye and the sense base of forms; likewise, it is the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, and the body and tangibles.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
What is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation and discernment of the sphere of mind?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates and discerns the sphere of mind, he forms this thought:”
Within the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), the sense-base of mind cannot be apprehended; the sense-base of mind has no fixed characteristic of entering, and the sense-base of mind has no root.

Why is this? The sense-base of mind arises from a multitude of causes and conditions and originates from inversion. It is bound to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as its object; through the conjunction of these two factors, it is able to perform its function. Thus, the sense-base of mind is caused by phenomena, arises depending on phenomena, and can be analyzed and explained in terms of phenomena.

These two are mutually dependent: the mind (*manas*) is the locus of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), and the mind is the gateway to the sphere of mental objects; conversely, the sphere of mental objects is the gateway to the mind. Therefore, it is called the "sphere of mental objects" because it is the gateway through which the mind enters its objects, and it is called the "mind-sphere" because it indicates the gateway through which the characteristics of the mind are manifested.

This is spoken according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); in its ultimate sense, the mind does not rely on dharmas, nor do dharmas rely on the mind. Because they arise through conditions and because all dharmas serve as conditions, one speaks of the "mind-base" (*manāyatana*). Because they arise through conditions and because they manifest the characteristics of the mind, one speaks of the "dharma-base" (*dharmāyatana*).

This is spoken in accordance with the delusions of worldly convention; within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) cannot be apprehended, nor can the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) be apprehended. When the wise seek among these bases, they do not perceive any reality.
"Whenever ordinary beings are associated with inversion, they describe these two bases—the mind-base and the phenomena-base—by means of dual characteristics.
These mind-base and phenomena-base are false and non-existent; because the Tathāgata has realized them as they truly are, he reveals these various bases."
Thus, these various bases arise from causes and conditions and are associated with inverted perceptions; herein, the mind-base and the phenomena-base are truly unobtainable.
Furthermore, the mind-base and the phenomena-base do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between.
