Furthermore, the mind-base (manāyatana) is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is only because it can perceive present causes and conditions that the mind-base and the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana) are spoken of, which is said in accordance with the minds of ordinary worldlings.

The wise person penetrates that these bases of mind and bases of phenomena are false and non-existent, arising from conceptualization, inversion, and discrimination; they are not bases, yet they are called bases. Why is this?
Within the various sense bases (*āyatana*), there is no fixed characteristic of a sense base.

The wise person penetrates that these sense bases are false and non-existent; they find that the intrinsic nature of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*) cannot be apprehended, nor can they apprehend any real characteristic arising from those mind-base and phenomena-base. These mind-base and phenomena-base arise merely through causes and conditions.

“The Tathāgata has taught that these sense-bases (āyatana) are characterized by the perception of knowing and seeing; yet these sense-bases are false and non-existent, associated with inverted views, and subject to various causes and conditions.”

The mind-base (manāyatana) and the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana) have no agent and no instigator; the mind-base does not know or discern the phenomena-base, nor does the phenomena-base know or discern the mind-base.

Why is this? Because both are devoid [of intrinsic nature]. If a dharma is devoid of characteristics, there is nothing therein to be differentiated. These sense bases (*āyatana*) all arise from causes and conditions; they are spoken of only in accordance with the inverted minds of ordinary beings.

"As the noble ones have realized: the sphere of mind and the sphere of phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going; the sphere of mind does not know the mind and does not discriminate the mind, and the sphere of phenomena does not know phenomena and does not discriminate phenomena, because both are empty and both are detached."
The mind does not know the nature of the mind, and phenomena do not know the nature of phenomena; these two natures are non-existent, and herein there is not a single determinate dharma.
The mind cannot establish itself nor can it destroy itself, and phenomena cannot establish themselves nor can they destroy themselves, because both are entirely non-existent.

The mind-base does not form the thought, "I am the mind-base," and the phenomena-base does not form the thought, "I am the phenomena-base. These two are both empty and like illusory appearances; they are merely conventional designations spoken of through conceptual differentiation.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates and discerns the sense-base of mind and the sense-base of phenomena in this way.
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s correct contemplation and discernment of the six internal sense-bases and the six external sense-bases?”

These so-called twelve bases (*āyatana*) are all false and illusory; they arise from a multitude of conditions and are associated with inversion. Because they possess two characteristics, they have internal and external applications.

Ordinary beings, not having heard the true Dharma and not knowing the suchness of the twelve bases as they truly are, become greedily attached to the eye-base, thinking, "I am the eye-base," or "The eye-base is mine";
they become greedily attached to the form-base, thinking, "I am the form-base," or "The form-base is mine."

It is the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*). [They think: "I am the mind-base (*manāyatana*)," "What belongs to me is the mind-base," "I am the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*)," and "What belongs to me is the dharma-base. Because of this greedy attachment, they are bound by the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) and run to and fro through the births and deaths of the five destinies, not knowing the path out.

"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva correctly contemplates these twelve bases (*āyatana*), he sees that these twelve bases are deceptive and not solid, empty and like the appearance of a phantom. He does not crave or cling to the eye-base as 'self' or 'mine,' nor does he crave or cling to the dharma-base as 'self' or 'mine. Because he does not crave or cling, he does not engage in recollective conceptualization."
In this way, the bodhisattva skillfully knows the twelve bases (*āyatana*). "Sustainer of the World!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains such skillful means regarding these bases, they are neither bound nor fettered by any of the twelve bases. They realize the nature of the bases while being able to discern them; they penetrate the twelve bases through the principle of dependent origination; they dismantle the twelve bases by means of the markless mark (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*); they do not fall into the path that relies upon these bases; they know that the nature of the bases is itself the absence of nature (*abhāva-svabhāva*); and they know the ultimate limit of the skillful means regarding the bases."
“World-Upholder!

It is like a mechanical device that draws water and sprinkles it in all four directions; the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are also like this. Through internal and external causes and conditions they are able to perform functions, yet within them no real entity can be found.”
These twelve bases (āyatana) are capable of performing actions because they are bound by the mechanisms of past karma.
"Sustaining the World!
What are called the 'bases' are the gateways through which all ordinary beings who lack knowledge and vision enter into affliction."
The eye is the gateway to forms, because it gives rise to craving and aversion.
Form is the gateway to the eye, because it gives rise to craving and aversion.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are gateways to phenomena, because they give rise to craving and aversion.
The Dharma is the gateway of the mind, for it gives rise to craving and aversion.
Thus, because these twelve bases are conjoined with craving and aversion, one does not know their true nature.
World-Holders!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand the nature of the sense bases (*āyatana*) therein; because they know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of these sense bases, they are not constrained by craving or aversion.
World-Holders!
In this way, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are skillfully knowledgeable regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Chapter Five: The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. "Holding the World! (Dharaṇīśvara)" [From the *Lokadhāraṇī-sūtra*]. Chapter Five: The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. "Holding the World! (Dharaṇīśvara)!"
What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully discerning and examining the twelve links of dependent origination?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva discerns and examines the twelve links of dependent origination as follows: because there is no existence, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*); because within ignorance there is no dharma, it is called ignorance; and because one does not know clarity, it is called ignorance.
What is meant by "not knowing illumination"?
Not knowing that the dharma of non-illumination is ultimately unattainable is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Why is this so?

It is said that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Although these volitional formations do not exist [independently], they are produced by ordinary beings; therefore, it is said that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations.
Because consciousness arises from volitional formations, it is said that volitional formations are the condition for consciousness.
Name-and-form consists of two aspects; therefore, it is said that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
From name-and-form arise the six sense bases; therefore, it is said that the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition.
From the six sense bases arises contact; therefore it is said that contact has the six sense bases as its condition.
From contact arises feeling; therefore it is said that feeling has contact as its condition.
From feeling arises craving; therefore it is said that craving has feeling as its condition.
From craving arises grasping; therefore, it is said that craving is the condition for grasping.
From grasping arises existence; therefore, it is said that grasping is the condition for existence.
From existence arises birth; therefore, it is said that existence is the condition for birth.

From birth, there arises the accumulation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair; therefore, it is said that with birth as condition, there is the accumulation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
Within this great mass of suffering and affliction, what dharma is being accumulated?

One should simply know that inversion is contrary to clarity; the accumulation of ignorance constitutes craving for future existence, which, relying on the defilement of delight, seeks birth in various places—this is the accumulation of craving.
“Holder of the World!
Such is the world: bound by the twelve links of dependent origination, blind and sightless, it enters the net of ignorance and falls into the midst of darkness.”
With ignorance as the primary cause, the twelve links of dependent origination arise in their entirety.
Bodhisattvas contemplate the true nature of ignorance in this way, and because they know that ignorance is empty, its ultimate beginning cannot be apprehended.

Why is this? Because ignorance does not exist, the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) does not exist. When the wise contemplate that which is not a limit as being the primordial limit, they do not conceptualize a primordial limit, for they have severed recollection, thought, and discrimination.
Not being greedily attached to ignorance, one knows that all dharmas are non-existent; these dharmas are not as they are described.

If one says that all dharmas are non-existent, this is precisely to say that there is no clarity in knowledge and vision; to be able to penetrate the non-existence of all dharmas is itself the attainment of clarity.
In this context, there is no other illumination; rather, knowing and seeing the absence of ignorance is what is called "illumination.
What is meant by knowing and seeing the absence of ignorance?

It refers to the fact that all phenomena are non-existent, all phenomena are unattainable, all phenomena are false and inverted, and all phenomena are not as they are described—this is called knowing and seeing the absence of ignorance.
To know and see that ignorance is itself illumination—
why is this? Because illumination has no inherent existence.

Regarding "with ignorance as a condition, there are volitional formations": all phenomena are non-existent; yet ordinary beings enter into the darkness of ignorance and, deluded and confused, produce various karmic actions. These karmic actions have no form and no location; it is not that ignorance can actually produce karmic actions, but because they arise and act despite the absence of any real dharma, it is said that "with ignorance as a condition, there are volitional formations."

All karmic formations (saṃskāra) have no accumulation; whether they come from this place or that place, these karmic formations are neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present. Ignorance is empty of the nature of ignorance, and karmic formations are empty of the nature of karmic formations. All karmic formations have no basis; they arise solely dependent upon ignorance.

The various karmic formations do not depend on ignorance, nor does ignorance depend on the karmic formations; ignorance does not know ignorance, and the karmic formations do not know the karmic formations. Thus, these ignorances and karmic formations arise from ignorance due to perversion. Within this, one cannot apprehend ignorance, nor can one apprehend the karmic formations; one cannot apprehend the nature of ignorance, nor can one apprehend the nature of the karmic formations. It is merely that, by way of the conventional designation of "darkness," it is called "darkness."
Because of this darkness of ignorance, it is analytically taught that karmic formations arise from non-existent phenomena; therefore, both ignorance and karmic formations are entirely non-existent.

Regarding "consciousness conditioned by volitional formations": consciousness does not depend on volitional formations, nor does consciousness arise apart from volitional formations; yet volitional formations do not produce consciousness. Why is this?

Karmic formations do not know karmic formations, nor is there anyone who brings karmic formations along; yet, through the inversion of sentient beings, consciousness arises from karmic formations. This consciousness is neither within karmic formations, nor outside of karmic formations, nor in between them.
This consciousness has no producer, nor is there anyone who causes it to arise; rather, consciousness arises solely because the continuity of karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) remains uninterrupted.

When the wise seek the characteristic of consciousness, they cannot find it; nor can they find the arising of consciousness. Consciousness does not know itself, nor does consciousness see itself; consciousness does not depend upon consciousness.

Regarding "consciousness is the condition for name-and-form": name-and-form does not depend upon consciousness, nor does name-and-form arise apart from consciousness; yet this name-and-form does not come from within consciousness, but exists only by depending on consciousness.
Ordinary worldlings, shrouded in darkness, crave and cling to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

yet consciousness does not even reach name-and-form. When the wise seek name-and-form here, it cannot be found and cannot be seen. This name-and-form is formless and directionless; it arises from recollection, thought, and conceptual discrimination. This characteristic of name-and-form exists because of consciousness as its condition; since the very nature of consciousness cannot be apprehended, how much less can name-and-form, which is produced through the condition of consciousness?
If it were certain that this nature of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) could be attained, such a thing would be impossible.

As for "the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) having name-and-form as their condition," these six sense bases arise with name-and-form as their cause; because "name" resides within the body, there are inhalations and exhalations that benefit the body as well as the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma). These six sense bases are all deceptive and non-existent, arising from conceptual discrimination (vikalpa) and possessing perverted functions.
"Regarding 'contact as the condition for the six sense bases,' this contact exists in dependence upon form, yet contact does not touch form. Why is this?
Form has no cognition;
it is no different from grass, trees, tiles, or stones. It is only because [contact] arises from the six sense bases that it is conventionally designated as 'contact' through discrimination."
Why is this? Since the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) themselves are empty, illusory, and non-existent, how much more so the contact (*sparśa*) that arises from them?

Contact is empty and non-existent, arising from conceptualization and inversion; it has no direction and no location. Because contact is empty due to the absence of an intrinsic nature of contact, contact does not know the six sense bases, nor do the six sense bases know contact.

"Regarding 'feeling conditioned by contact,' this feeling does not exist within contact, nor does it exist outside of contact, nor does it exist in between. Furthermore, contact does not carry feeling from elsewhere; rather, feeling arises from contact. Since contact itself is illusory and non-existent, how much more so is the feeling that arises from contact?"

No sensation possesses a single determinate characteristic; all sensations are non-existent. They arise from inversion and function through inversion. Regarding "craving has sensation as its condition":

this sensation does not bring craving from another place, nor does sensation unite with craving. Sensation does not know craving, nor does it differentiate craving; craving does not know sensation, nor does it differentiate sensation; craving does not unite with sensation.

This craving does not depend upon feeling, nor does craving exist apart from feeling; since even within feeling the characteristic of feeling cannot be found, how much less can craving arise through the conditions of feeling?

Craving is not within feeling, not without feeling, and not in between; craving is also not within craving itself, not outside of craving, and not in between. Within craving, the characteristic of craving is unattainable; this craving is merely called "craving" because it corresponds with false conceptualization and inversion.

This craving is neither past, nor future, nor present; this craving does not arise by way of the characteristic of bondage, nor is this craving itself the characteristic of bondage. Rather, it is because the continuity of causes and conditions is uninterrupted that one speaks of "craving conditioned by feeling."
The wise one knows and sees that this craving has no location and no direction; it is empty, lacking solidity, false, and non-existent. Regarding "clinging arises with craving as its condition":

craving does not bring clinging from another place, nor does craving unite with clinging, nor can craving produce clinging. It is because craving exists that it is called clinging; it is spoken of only in accordance with the conjunction of conditions.

Grasping does not unite with craving nor is it separated from it; craving does not unite with grasping nor is it separated from it. Grasping is not within craving, nor is it outside of craving, nor is it in between them. Since craving itself does not even exist, how much less can there be grasping produced through the condition of craving?
The definitive characteristics of all grasping (*upādāna*) cannot be found.

The wise know and see that this grasping is false and non-existent; within grasping there is no characteristic of grasping. This grasping is not of the past, future, or present; it is neither inside grasping, nor outside grasping, nor in between. This grasping arises solely from inversion; it is produced by primary causes and conditions, and exists now because of various conditions.
There is no dharma that is either joined or dispersed; this grasping has no root, and no fixed dharma can be found.
Ordinary beings undergo this false grasping because all these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are false.
The world is bound by grasping; the wise person penetrates that this grasping is false, empty, and without solidity, having no root and no fixed dharma to be found.

Regarding "existence conditioned by clinging": this clinging does not bring existence with it, nor can this clinging produce existence; yet it is said that "existence is conditioned by clinging. This existence is neither within clinging, nor outside clinging, nor in between them.

There is existence that does not depend on grasping; grasping neither joins with existence nor separates from it. It is only because of the harmony of various conditions that one speaks of existence having grasping as its condition.

Grasping cannot produce existence, and grasping does not differentiate existence. Since grasping itself is illusory and non-existent, how much more so existence produced through the conditions of grasping?

There is that which is neither existent nor non-existent; it cannot be apprehended within the intermediate state; it is not within, it is not without, and it is not in between; this existence is neither of the past, the future, nor the present.
The wise person penetrates that existence is illusory; it is associated with inversion, neither conjoined nor dispersed.

There is nothing known and nothing to be discriminated; this existence has no location and no direction. This existence has no prior limit, no posterior limit, and no middle limit. Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, yet because it accords with the twelve links of dependent origination, it is said to exist.
The wise person penetrates that existence is empty of characteristics and lacks solidity.

That which arises through causes and conditions does not bring existence with it when it arises; nor does arising conjoin with or disperse from existence. This arising is neither within existence, nor without existence, nor in between them.

Existence cannot give rise to birth, nor does it exist apart from the arising of existence; rather, it merely demonstrates the continuity of the twelve links of dependent origination and is spoken of as "arising through causes and conditions.
Existence and birth are neither related by causal condition nor unrelated; since even existence itself cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be the arising of birth from existence?

The wise person penetrates this arising as not being dependent on the existence of arising; within arising there is no characteristic of arising, within arising there is no intrinsic nature, within arising there is no fundamental basis, and no fixed dharma can be apprehended.

The wise person penetrates the fact that this birth is without intrinsic nature and non-existent; it merely demonstrates the continuous succession of the conjunction of the twelve links of dependent origination, and therefore it is said that there is "arising through causes and conditions."

Birth is a non-existent dharma, neither conjoined nor dispersed; birth is not within existence, not without existence, nor in between. This birth is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present. The prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit of this birth cannot be apprehended. The root of this birth cannot be apprehended. The wise penetrate that it arises from a multitude of causes and conditions, corresponding with inversion, being empty, false, and non-existent, like the appearance of a magical illusion.

"Regarding birth as the condition for aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair: it is not that birth brings aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair along with it; nor is it that birth can actually produce aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair."
Old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction do not exist within birth, nor do they exist outside of birth, nor do they exist in between.

Old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction likewise do not depend upon birth; yet, because of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction can be spoken of—this is merely to demonstrate the dharma of dependent origination through various causes and conditions.

Birth does not conjoin with nor disperse from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; since even birth itself cannot be apprehended within birth, how much less so can the suffering and affliction of old age and death that have birth as their causal condition?
Within the suffering and affliction of old age and death, the suffering and affliction of old age and death cannot be found. Why is this?
The suffering and affliction of old age and death does not exist within the suffering and affliction of old age and death, nor does it exist outside of it, nor does it exist in between.

The suffering and affliction of old age and death are neither past, nor future, nor present; the suffering and affliction of old age and death do not unite with old age and death, nor do they disperse from them. Rather, through association with inversion and the convergence of various conditions, the twelve links of dependent origination are fulfilled; therefore, it is said that birth is the condition for the suffering and affliction of old age and death.

The suffering and affliction of old age and death have no basis; the definitive characteristic of the suffering and affliction of old age and death cannot be found; and the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit of the suffering and affliction of old age and death cannot be found.

The wise person penetrates the suffering and affliction of old age and death as being false and non-existent, associated with inversion, devoid of a fundamental basis, uncreated, unarisen, and unborn.

“Observing the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination in this way, one does not perceive the dharma of dependent origination—whether past, future, or present—and nor does one perceive the characteristics of dependent origination.”

One should know that causes and conditions are themselves without conditions; they are without birth, without marks, without action, without arising, and without root, because from the very beginning, all phenomena have never existed.
One penetrates these twelve links of dependent origination and also perceives that within these twelve links of dependent origination there is no agent and no experiencer.

Since a phenomenon arises from causes, when those causes are absent, the phenomenon is also absent; thus, because the Bodhisattva follows the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*), all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Entering into such contemplation, that which is without conditions is itself the twelve links of dependent origination; herein, nothing is produced.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as a false arising, and by conforming to the meaning of ignorance, he penetrates the twelve links of dependent origination.

If a phenomenon does not exist, that phenomenon is also non-existent; therefore, it is said that by conforming to the meaning of ignorance, one penetrates the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance is non-arising, non-acting, and non-emerging; it has no root, no fixed dharma, and is without conditions or anything whatsoever.

At that time, the bodhisattva does not discriminate between this as "knowledge" and this as "ignorance. The true reality (*dharmatā*) of ignorance is itself knowledge. Because of ignorance, all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent; all phenomena are without conditions and without conceptualization or discrimination. Therefore, by conforming to the meaning of ignorance, one penetrates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom of skillful means regarding the twelve links of dependent origination.
If a bodhisattva can thus penetrate the conjunction and dissolution of the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called the bodhisattva’s excellent attainment of the wisdom of non-arising.”

Why is this? Because if one contemplates through the lens of arising and ceasing, one cannot properly understand the twelve links of dependent origination; however, if one contemplates the gathering and dispersing of the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called attaining the wisdom of non-arising.
If one attains the wisdom of non-arising, this is called penetrating the twelve links of dependent origination.
"World-Upholder!

Therefore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter into penetration and wishes to realize the wisdom of non-arising, they should diligently practice and cultivate this wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination; thus, they will be able to contemplate and realize the mark of non-arising within the twelve links of dependent origination."
“Dhāraṇīdhara!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that non-arising is itself the twelve links of dependent origination, he will be able to attain such skillful means regarding the twelve links of dependent origination. This person, through the mark of non-arising, perceives and sees the triple world, and swiftly attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.”

It should be known that this bodhisattva has received the proximate prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from all the Buddhas currently existing; before long, this bodhisattva shall receive the prediction and receive it in successive order.

“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! Such a virtuous person, by virtue of receiving this prediction, attains a mind of peace and security; among all the methods for understanding the intent of the dharmas, they attain the light of wisdom. This person penetrates the twelve links of dependent origination as being unborn; this person draws near to the Buddhas of the present; this person has no fear of the various evil Māras; this person crosses the stream of birth and death and reaches dry land; this person crosses the mire of ignorance and reaches the place of peace and security.”

“Lokadhara! Whether in my present life or after my parinirvāṇa, if anyone hears, believes, recites, or cultivates these skillful means of the twelve links of dependent origination, I shall bestow upon that person the prediction that before long they will attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). I also predict that before long this person shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas currently living.”
Chapter Six: The Four Foundations of Mindfulness. The *Lokadhātusthiti-sūtra*, Chapter Six: The Four Foundations of Mindfulness. The Buddha told Lokadhātusthiti:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who skillfully knows the four foundations of mindfulness?"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates and discerns the four foundations of mindfulness:
observing the body in accordance with the body, observing feelings in accordance with feelings, observing the mind in accordance with the mind, and observing phenomena in accordance with phenomena.
"What is meant by 'contemplating the body as it truly is' and 'contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as they truly are'? "Dhāraṇīdhara!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the body as it truly is, he contemplates the characteristics of the body as they really are: namely, that this body is impermanent, suffering, like a disease, like an ulcer; it is characterized by affliction, distress, grief, decay, movement, and disintegration. This body is impure and loathsome, a vessel of foul secretions; its interior is filled with various kinds of filth, and from its nine orifices, foul and stinking matter constantly flows. The impurity of the body is like a walking latrine."

When observing the body in this manner, one finds not even a single hair’s breadth of purity within it that is not loathsome. One knows that this body is a skeletal structure bound by sinews and wrapped in skin and flesh, arisen from the karmic causes and conditions of past actions, and fettered by the accumulation of grasping.
What is accumulation?
What is grasping?
That this body arises from prior causes and conditions is called grasping.
Now, bathing, food and drink, clothing, bedding, mattresses, and medicine—these are called "origination.
Thus, through present conditions as origination, one is bound by grasping; yet, by the power of the retribution of past karma, they remain functional.
Furthermore, this body is composed of the four great elements and lacks any fixed reality; it is comprised within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and is conventionally designated as "body.
Why is it called "body"? Because it is capable of performing actions, it is called "body."
Because it is the basis for attachment and clinging, it is called "body" (kāya).
Because it functions according to one's will, it is called "body.
Because it arises from recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, it is called "body."
Because it is a provisional combination [of parts], it is called a "body.
Because it is conjoined with karma, it is called a "body.
This body will before long end in ruin and decay; it is impermanent, unstable, and characterized by change.
This body does not exist within the body, nor does it exist outside the body, nor does it exist in between. This body does not know the body, nor does it see the body.

This body is without action, without movement, and without aspiration; it is also without mind, being no different from grass, trees, tiles, or stones. Within this body, there is no definitive characteristic of a self.
"Thus, by correctly contemplating and discerning the body, one knows that it has no agent, nor any instigator; this body has no prior limit, no posterior limit, and no middle limit."
This body possesses not a single mark of permanence, stability, or solidity; it is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped or touched.

This body is the dwelling place of eighty thousand worms; this body is afflicted by a hundred kinds of diseases. Because of the three types of suffering, this body is suffering; there is no one to save it—namely, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). This body is a vessel for manifold sufferings.
"When observing the body in this way, one further reflects: 'This body is not self, nor does it belong to another;

it lacks autonomy and cannot act as it pleases, performing this or refraining from that. This body has no fundamental basis and no fixed dharma can be found; the nature of this body is empty, devoid of any definitive characteristic.'"

This body arises from falsehood and is bound by the workings of mechanical contrivances; it originates from the causal conditions of fundamental karma. One should not give rise to notions of "self" or "mine" regarding this body, nor should we cherish our bodies or our lives.

"When the Bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he does not perceive the body as either joined or dispersed; he does not see anything from which it comes, to which it goes, or any place where it dwells."

Not discriminating whether this body is past, future, or present, one does not rely upon the life of the body; one does not covet or cherish the body as "I" or "mine," and remains constantly detached from bodily sensations.

This bodhisattva contemplates the body as empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self, because within this body neither a self nor anything belonging to a self can be found; thus, the characteristics of this body cannot be apprehended.
If this bodhisattva does not perceive the marks of a body, they do not wish for the body to enter [the path], nor does the body arise as the practice of the Way.

What is meant by "entering"? This body has no agent and no originator; it possesses neither the mark of acting nor the mark of arising. It is born from a multitude of causes and conditions, and these causes and conditions can bring the body into combination. Yet these causes and conditions are also deceptive and non-existent; they correspond to inversion, being empty, without substance, and lacking solidity.
Furthermore, it is by these very causes and conditions that this body is produced; yet these causes and conditions themselves are without production and without marks.

Contemplating the body in this way, one enters into the mark of the non-production of the body. Having entered therein, one contemplates the body as being without marks, observing the body through the mark of marklessness. One knows that this body is without marks because no marks can be apprehended, and thus it is without production.
This body cannot be apprehended through past characteristics, future characteristics, or present characteristics. Why is this?
Because this body has no fundamental basis and no fixed dharma can be apprehended; whether as "this" or "that," this body cannot be found.
When observing in this way, one knows that the body comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; thus, one enters the path of the body’s non-arising and non-ceasing.
“World-Holders!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus contemplates the body in accordance with the body and enters the mark of reality, they are able to sever desire and defilement regarding the body, swiftly causing their mindfulness to dwell correctly within the body. This is called ‘contemplating the body in accordance with the body.’”
“Holder of the World!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of feelings in accordance with their reception?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.”

One perceives these three types of sensation as coming from nowhere and going nowhere; they are merely the conjunction of false conditions, sustained by the retribution of past karma and associated with inversion. One knows that all sensations are false, arising from recollection, thought, and discrimination.
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates all sensations (*vedanā*): he does not apprehend past sensation, he does not apprehend future sensation, and he does not apprehend present sensation.
This bodhisattva sees that all past sensations are empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self, impermanent, lacking solidity, and without any characteristic of changelessness.

Thus one contemplates these past sensations as having the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of quiescence, and the characteristic of signlessness; one contemplates future sensations as empty, without self and without what belongs to a self, impermanent, unstable, and lacking solidity, and as having no characteristic of changelessness.
He contemplates all future sensations as having the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of quiescence, and the characteristic of signlessness.
When this bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he forms this thought:
"All sensations lack a determinate characteristic; they have no root and no fixed nature. Because they are not identical, they arise and perish anew at every moment without a time of abiding."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"These various sensations are without action and without an agent; they arise merely within the minds of ordinary people associated with inverted views as three kinds of sensation. Belonging to the causes of past karma, these various sensations exist now due to the convergence of present conditions. All these sensations are empty and lack solidity; they are false dharmas, like an empty fist."
Observing sensation in this way, the mind abides in a single point.

At that time, the Bodhisattva attains penetration into the characteristics of the arising, subsiding, and cessation of all sensations; he sees that all sensations are neither conjoined nor dispersed, and furthermore, he does not perceive sensation within sensation. He then reflects:
"All sensations are empty, because their nature is empty."
He immediately attained penetration into the mark of non-arising of all sensations.
These sensations are without arising, without cessation, and without the mark of formation; these sensations are all without marks and without the mark of formation.

Reflecting in this way, one is able to remain unattached when experiencing any sensation; one knows and sees the characteristics of all sensations as they truly are, becomes detached from all that is felt, and finds no dependence even upon these sensations. When the mind completely relinquishes itself toward all sensations, one swiftly attains the *śamatha-samādhi* (the samādhi of equanimity).
“Holder of the World!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates feelings in this way, observing them in accordance with their reception.
Holder of the World!”
What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva observing the mind in accordance with the mind?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes the characteristics of the arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing of the mind.
When observing in this way, they form this thought:

"This mind comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it arises merely through the conditions of perceived objects. It has no root and no fixed dharma that can be apprehended; this mind has no coming, no going, and no abiding or changing that can be apprehended."
This mind is neither past, future, nor present; because this mind cognizes objects, it arises from recollection; this mind is not within, not without, and not in between.

This mind has not a single characteristic of arising; this mind is without intrinsic nature and without fixedness. There is no one who gives rise to it, nor is there anyone who causes it to arise; it is called "mind" because it gives rise to various karmas.

It is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is able to cognize various objects; it is called "mind" because it arises and ceases moment by moment in an uninterrupted succession, merely causing sentient beings to penetrate the characteristics of mental objects.

Within the mind there is no characteristic of mind; this mind, from its very origin, is unborn and unarisen, its nature being eternally pure. It is only because it is defiled by adventitious afflictions that discrimination arises.
The mind does not know the mind, nor does it see the mind.
Why is this? Because this mind is empty; its nature is inherently empty, for fundamentally it has no existence whatsoever.
This mind has no fixed dharma, for a fixed dharma cannot be apprehended.

This mind has no phenomena that are either conjoined or dispersed; this mind’s prior limit cannot be apprehended, its posterior limit cannot be apprehended, and its middle limit cannot be apprehended. This mind is formless and there is no one who can see it; the mind does not see itself, nor does it know its own nature.
Whenever ordinary beings are associated with inversion, it arises because they perceive the characteristics of consciousness through false conditions.
This mind is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self; it is impermanent, unstable, and not solid; it lacks any characteristic of unchanging nature.
Reflecting in this way, one attains the mindfulness of mental objects that accords with the mind.

At that time, such a person does not discriminate whether this mind is "mind" or "not-mind," but simply well understands that the mind has the characteristic of non-arising, thereby penetrating the nature of the mind's non-arising.
Why is this? Because the mind has no determinate nature, nor does it have determinate characteristics.

When the wise person penetrates the fact that this mind is unborn and signless, they then contemplate the arising, gathering, dispersing, and ceasing of the mind as it truly is. Contemplating in this way, they do not apprehend any characteristic of the mind’s gathering or its ceasing; they no longer discriminate whether the mind ceases or does not cease, yet they are able to attain the mark of the true purity of the mind.
“By means of this pure mind, the Bodhisattva cannot be afflicted by adventitious defilements. Why is this?

Because the Bodhisattva perceives and knows the characteristic of the purity of his own mind, and likewise knows the characteristic of the purity of the minds of sentient beings; he then forms this thought:”
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.

When contemplating in this way, one does not apprehend the characteristic of mental defilement, nor does one apprehend the characteristic of mental purity; one simply knows that this mind is always characterized by purity.
“Holding the World!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus contemplates the mind with a compliant mind.
Holding the World!”
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of phenomena in accordance with the Dharma?

The bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena and does not perceive them internally, nor externally, nor in between; furthermore, they do not apprehend any phenomena as belonging to the past, the future, or the present.

One should simply know that all phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions and originate from inversion; that all phenomena lack any determinate characteristic, such as the notion that "these phenomena belong to this person. The intrinsic nature of phenomena does not exist as phenomena within phenomena, nor do phenomena exist within phenomena, nor outside of phenomena, nor in between them.
All phenomena do not conjoin with one another, nor do they disperse; all phenomena have no root and no fixed characteristic, because all phenomena are non-existent.
They are unmoving and unconditioned, because all phenomena are like space and non-existent.
All phenomena are deceptive and like illusions, because the characteristics of illusion do not exist.
All phenomena have the characteristic of eternal purity, because they are all undefiled.
All phenomena have the characteristic of non-appropriation, because all sensations do not exist.
All phenomena are like dreams, for the nature of dreams is non-existent.
All phenomena are formless, for form is non-existent.
All phenomena are like reflections, for their nature is eternally non-existent.
All phenomena are without name and without mark, because names and marks do not exist.
All phenomena are like echoes, because they are falsely constructed and lack any inherent existence.
All dharmas are without intrinsic nature, because such a nature cannot be apprehended.
All dharmas are like a mirage, for they are known to be non-existent.

When a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas in this way, he does not perceive any dharma as having either a single characteristic or diverse characteristics; nor does he perceive any dharma as being joined with or separated from another dharma, nor does he perceive any dharma as depending upon another dharma.
When observing in this way, one sees that all phenomena come from nowhere, nor does one see any place where all phenomena abide.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without abiding, without support, and without arising; all phenomena have no place of abiding, because such a place does not exist and cannot be apprehended.
“Lokadhara! All dharmas are without differentiation; all dharmas have no characteristic of discrimination. They function only because of the delusions of sentient beings.
These dharmas have no location and no direction; the wise realize that all dharmas do not have a single characteristic, nor a dual characteristic, nor a distinct characteristic.”
Why is this? World-Upholder!
All dharmas are unarisen, uncreated, and unproduced; there is no creator of them. All dharmas are devoid of a root; all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, for they transcend all natures.
All phenomena have no place of refuge, because all places of refuge are non-existent.
Observing all phenomena in this way, one skillfully knows that they are without self and without person, and discerns that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
All these phenomena are empty, because their nature is inherently empty.
All phenomena are signless, because no signs are perceived; thus, one does not give rise to aspirations regarding any phenomena.
At that moment, one contemplates and discerns that all phenomena are unarisen, and forms this thought:
"In this, there is truly no dharma that arises or ceases. When one contemplates in this way, the mind abides in a single point;

at that time, one attains penetration into the non-arising of all dharmas, and one also comes to know and see the accumulation, exhaustion, and cessation of all dharmas, and is further able to enter into the state where all dharmas are devoid of marks and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Why is this? World-Upholder!
All dharmas lack a determinate nature; the wise penetrate all dharmas as being signless and devoid of signs.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate dharmas in accordance with the Dharma.

Contemplating in this way, they attain nothing regarding dharmas and grasp nothing regarding dharmas; they practice not for the sake of the arising of dharmas, nor for their abiding, nor for their cessation, yet they perceive all dharmas as having the characteristic of total extinction and the characteristic of quiescent extinction.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
For what reason are they called ‘foundations of mindfulness’ (smṛtyupasthāna)?”

The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are the fact that all dharmas have no location; they have no place of arising and no place of existence. To be able to enter into all dharmas in this way so that mindfulness is not distracted is called the foundations of mindfulness.

Furthermore, regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): they are the state of knowing and seeing all phenomena as they truly are—neither abiding, nor arising, nor grasped. This is called the foundations of mindfulness. Chapter Seven:
The Chapter on the Five Faculties (*pañcendriya*) from the *Lokadhātṛ-sūtra*. "Holding the World! (Dharaṇīdhara!)”
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge of the faculties?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva correctly contemplates the five supramundane faculties.
What are these five?
These are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

When a bodhisattva cultivates these five faculties, they believe that all phenomena arise from a multitude of causes and conditions; they are produced by inversion and are the union of false conditions, resembling a whirling firebrand or the nature of a dream.

One believes that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, impure, and without self; they are like a disease and like an ulcer, lacking any solidity, being deceptive, unreal, and characterized by decay and disintegration.

Furthermore, one has faith that all phenomena are false and non-existent, like an empty fist or the variegated colors of a rainbow that deceive small children; they exist only through conceptualization and discrimination as provisional borrowings, lacking any essential substance or fixed nature.

Furthermore, one has faith that all dharmas are neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present; one has faith that all dharmas come from nowhere and go nowhere; one has faith that all dharmas are empty, signless, and wishless; one has faith that all dharmas are unarisen, uncreated, unoriginated, signless, and free from all signs; and one has faith in the purity of ethical discipline, the purity of meditative concentration, the purity of wisdom, the purity of liberation, and the purity of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"When a bodhisattva thus accomplishes the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and attains non-retrogression, because faith is primary, they are able to faithfully uphold the precepts.

This faith is constantly non-retrogressive and non-declining; having accomplished the dharma of non-retrogression, they abide immovably. Within this faith, they always follow the retribution of karma and become a person who has accomplished faith. They sever all false views and do not seek teachers apart from the Dharma, but take only the Buddhas as their teachers. Constantly following the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they know that the Sangha practices the right path. Abiding in pure precepts, they accomplish patience. Having attained such immovable and indestructible faith, and because this superior faith increases, it is called 'accomplishing the faculty of faith.'"

“Lokadhara! What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s right contemplation of the faculty of diligence, the accomplishment of the faculty of diligence, and the skillful knowledge of the faculty of diligence?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence without ceasing or resting, constantly desiring to eliminate the five hindrances, and exerts diligence even to the point of hearing such profound dharmas as these, this is called diligence.”

This bodhisattva seeks the Dharma without ceasing or resting, with diligence that does not retreat; furthermore, because they wish to sever all obstructing dharmas, they practice diligence with tireless vigor; they also practice diligence to sever various evil, unwholesome, and afflictive dharmas; and they likewise practice diligence to increase various wholesome dharmas.
This bodhisattva resolutely accomplishes diligence; without being greedily attached to this diligence, they enter into this impartial diligence and achieves non-retrogressive diligence.

This person employs correct means, exerting diligence in order to penetrate all dharmas; within that diligence, they do not follow others, and through the clarity of wisdom attained within diligence, they achieve the mark of non-retrogression.
Because they are able to attain such non-retrogressive and superior diligence, they are said to have accomplished the faculty of diligence.
"World-Holder!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to attain the faculty of mindfulness?"
Having well cultivated the faculty of mindfulness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly gathers his mindfulness in one place;
he practices generosity with gentleness and fulfills the holy life (*brahmacarya*), upholding ultimately pure morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he constantly reflects upon the purity of his physical, verbal, and mental actions, and always—
One should contemplate the ultimate nature of things; one should constantly contemplate the skillful means regarding the characteristics of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing of all phenomena;
one should constantly contemplate the knowledge and vision of the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;

one should constantly contemplate the skillful means regarding the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, the path, meditative concentrations, liberations, and various samādhis; and one should constantly contemplate that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.
One should not create or give rise to that which has the characteristic of being ineffable; one should constantly contemplate the desire to attain the wisdom of non-arising,
constantly contemplate the desire to attain the perfection of the wisdom of patience, constantly contemplate the wisdom of detachment and the wisdom of cessation,
constantly contemplate the desire to attain the fullness of the Buddha-dharma, and constantly contemplate ensuring that the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not enter the mind.
He constantly contemplates unimpeded wisdom, and this mindfulness is ever-undiminished, never lost, and never regressed;
entering into such contemplation, he does not follow others.
Because this person has attained such firm and superior mindfulness, he is said to have accomplished the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to attain the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) and being able to attain the skillful means (*upāya*) for the faculty of concentration?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) within the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*), yet does not rely upon that concentration nor crave it. He skillfully grasps the characteristics of concentration, skillfully attains the liberation of the skillful means for concentration, skillfully generates concentration, and is also able to practice objectless concentration (*anālambana-dhyāna*).”

They fully know all gateways of meditative concentration; they are skilled in entering meditative concentration, skilled in abiding in meditative concentration, and skilled in arising from meditative concentration, yet they do not rely upon meditative concentration.

He skillfully knows the characteristics of the objects of focus and skillfully knows the characteristics of the conditions; furthermore, he does not greedily crave the flavor of dhyāna, but sports with mastery among all meditative concentrations without following others, nor is he reborn according to those dhyānas.
Having attained mastery over all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), one does not regard them as difficult or trivial, but acts according to one's will.

Because such a person has attained this superior meditative concentration (*adhipati-dhyāna*), they are said to have attained the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) and the skillful means for attaining that faculty of concentration.
“Holder of the World!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishing the faculty of wisdom and attaining the skillful means of the faculty of wisdom?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish the penetration of the faculty of wisdom, which is to say, they are able to correctly extinguish all sufferings.”

This person accomplishes the wisdom of thorough penetration; in all circumstances and applications, they attain detachment from contemplation and relinquish contemplation, thereby accomplishing the wisdom that accords with *nirvāṇa*.

Because they have accomplished this faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), they well know that the triple world is entirely ablaze and well know that the triple world is entirely suffering; by means of this wisdom, they do not dwell within the triple world.

This person contemplates and discerns that all things within the three realms are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unconditioned, and non-originated; seeing the path that transcends all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they apply themselves with diligent vigor as if their head or clothing were on fire, for the sake of fulfilling all the Buddha-dharmas.

The wisdom of this bodhisattva cannot be obstructed or destroyed; by means of this penetrating wisdom, they are able to transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*) and do not rely upon the phenomena of the triple world. They sever all delight in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and their minds harbor no craving for any dharmas that are subject to defilement, attachment, or bondage. Their minds are weary of and detached from the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), and their minds do not dwell in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) or formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). They achieve superior wisdom and accomplish immeasurable merit like the great ocean; through this wisdom, they encounter no doubt or difficulty regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) within all dharmas.

By means of this wisdom, this person penetrates the three realms; with a mind unattached within the three realms, because they have attained this superior wisdom, it is called the faculty of transcendent wisdom, and they have attained the skillful means of the faculty of wisdom.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! For what reason are they called ‘roots’ (mūla)? They are called roots because of their sense of sovereignty;

they are called roots because of their immovability; they are called roots because they cannot be destroyed; they are called roots because they cannot be made to regress; they are called roots because they do not follow after others; they are called roots because they are non-retrogressive; they are called roots because they cannot be led astray; they are called roots because they accord with the True Dharma; they are called roots because they are free from greedy attachment; they are called roots because they are unmixed.”
"Furthermore, *Lokadhara*!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully knows the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings and is also able to skillfully train in the discernment of those faculties.
The bodhisattva knows the faculties of sentient beings who are stained by desire, and knows the faculties of sentient beings who are free from the stain of desire;..."
He knows the faculties of sentient beings who are prone to anger, and he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are free from anger;
he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are prone to delusion, and he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are free from delusion;

he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are about to fall into the evil realms, he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are about to be born among humans, and he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are about to be born in the heavens.
He knows the faculties of sentient beings with soft minds;
he knows the faculties of superior, middling, and inferior sentient beings;
and he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are degenerate and those who are not degenerate.
He knows the faculties of sentient beings regarding those who practice with diligence and those who do not;
he knows the faculties of sentient beings regarding those who are skillful and those who are unskillful.

He knows the faculties of sentient beings regarding those with faults and those without faults, those with defilements and those without defilements; he knows those who are prone to anger and resentment and those who are not; he knows those who are compliant and those who are not; and he knows those faculties that are obstructed and those that are unobstructed.
He knows the conduct of the desire realm; he knows the faculties of sentient beings regarding the conduct of the form realm and the formless realm.
He knows those with thick roots of goodness and those with thin roots of goodness; he knows the faculties of sentient beings who are fixed, unfixed, or wrongly fixed.

He knows those who are stingy and greedy and those who are free from stinginess and greed; he knows those who are frivolous and those who are not frivolous; he knows those who are deluded and those who are not deluded; he knows those who are flighty and those who are not flighty; he knows those who are wrathful and impatient, and those who are gentle and patient; he knows those with deep-seated stinginess and those who possess the faculty of complete generosity.

“He knows those who have faith and those who lack faith; he knows those who are respectful and those who are disrespectful; he knows those who fully maintain the precepts and those who maintain the precepts purely;

he knows those who possess patience; he knows the indolent and the diligent; he knows those with distracted minds and those who have attained concentration; he knows those without wisdom and those with wisdom; he knows the dull-witted and those who are not dull-witted; he knows those with overweening pride and those without overweening pride; he knows those who walk the right path and those who walk the wrong path; and he knows those with forgetfulness and those who have attained mindfulness and settled wisdom.”

He knows the faculties that are distracted and the faculties that are concentrated; he knows the impaired faculties and the unimpaired faculties; he knows the pure faculties and the impure faculties; he knows the luminous faculties; he knows the faculties that give rise to the Hīnayāna, the faculties that give rise to the Pratyekabuddhayāna, the faculties of all Bodhisattvas, and the faculties that give rise to the Buddhayāna.

This bodhisattva attains such skillful means for the discernment of the various faculties; because he does not follow others in these skillful means regarding the wisdom that discerns the faculties of such sentient beings, he is said to have "attained the skillful means of the faculties. He is also called "one who is not led by others," "one who is indestructible," "one who is non-retrogressive," "one who has attained the power of skillful means," "one who has attained the human faculties," and "one who has attained the faculties of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. He is also called "one who has attained supreme mastery," "one who is unbreakable and immovable," and "one who has reached the other shore."
One who accomplishes such merit will swiftly attain the power of mastery over all phenomena.
*Lokadhāri Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Lokadhāri Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Eightfold Noble Path. *Lokadhara-sūtra*, Chapter Eight: The Eightfold Noble Path.
"Lokadhara! [Listen.]”
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is well able to know the path, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells securely within the path?
What constitutes the path?
It refers to the eightfold noble path:
Right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
“World-Upholder!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being said to practice the eightfold noble path?
What is meant by attaining the skillful means of the eightfold noble path?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva attains right view and dwells in right view; they practice the path for the sake of severing all views, and they dwell in the path for the sake of severing all views, even up to the view of nirvāṇa and the view of a buddha.
Why is this? World-Upholder!
All views whatsoever are called false, even including the view of nirvana and the view of a Buddha.
Because it destroys all attachment to various views, it is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, being without views and without grasping at views—neither recollecting nor being attached to them, not taking them as objects, not engaging in them, and not discriminating among any views—is what is called right view.
What is it that this right view perceives?
It perceives that all worlds are false and inverted, bound by various views. When one perceives in this way, it is called abiding in the severance of all views;

regarding this right view as well, one does not dwell upon it, does not perceive it, and does not cling to or discriminate it—even down to the view of nirvāṇa or the view of the Buddha—one acts for the sake of the non-arising of all views.
"What is called right view?
All phenomena are quiescent; the marks of mindfulness are neither arising nor ceasing, being identical to nirvana.

Thus, one does not mindfully conceptualize all phenomena, nor do such non-conceptualizations manifest before the mind. Without being correct or deviant, without grasping or rejecting—this is called supramundane right view."
Why is it called supramundane right view?
Because such a person neither attains the mundane nor the supramundane; having transcended the world, they are free from all discrimination. Therefore, it is called supramundane right view.

One with right view perceives the world as it truly is, and perceives the supramundane in the same way; such a person no longer discriminates between "this is the world" and "this is the supramundane. Having severed all recollections and conceptual discriminations, this is called supramundane right view.
This person neither perceives the false nor perceives the correct; having severed all mental conceptions, this is called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, regarding right view, there is no further differentiation among all phenomena; for this reason, it is called right view.
Furthermore, right view is to know the meaning of all wrong views as they truly are.
Moreover, right view is to contemplate all wrong views as being equal.
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in right view.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in right view, they know right thought as it truly is and form this thought:
‘All thoughts are erroneous; even the thought of nirvāṇa and the thought of the Buddha are all erroneous thoughts.’”
Why is this? The severance of all conceptual discriminations is called right reflection.
That which is without conceptual discrimination is called right discernment; the severance of conceptual discrimination is right discernment.

Why is this? Because once such a person has known and seen all marks of conceptualization, they are no longer subject to error; they no longer discriminate between "this" and "that," but abide within such right discrimination, wherein they can no longer find any further discrimination, whether correct or erroneous.
Because such a person is free from all conceptualization and has transcended all conceptualization, they are said to possess right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Right reflection means discerning and seeing that all conceptualizations are false, unreal, and arise from inversion; within all conceptualizations, there is no conceptualization.

This person dwells securely in right reflection; they no longer engage in discrimination between what is correct and what is erroneous. Because they have abandoned all discrimination, transcended all discrimination, and severed all discrimination, it is called "right discrimination."
At that time, this person is not bound by any conceptual constructions, because they know and see that the nature of all conceptual constructions is equal; this is called abiding in right reflection.

“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently accumulates right speech (*samyagvāc*). This person sees that all speech is false and unreal, arising from inversion; it is merely a product of recollection and conceptualization, existing through various causes and conditions. He forms this thought:
‘The characteristic of speech cannot be found within speech itself. To extinguish all speech and to know all vocal karma as it truly is—this is called right speech.”
These words come from nowhere and go nowhere; one who can see them thus is said to possess right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
At that time, such a person abides within the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and whatever they utter is all right speech; therefore, it is said that they abide in right speech.
This person abides in the foremost purity of verbal action; they also know and see the characteristics of all verbal actions and penetrate all languages.
What this person speaks is never erroneous; therefore, they are said to abide in right speech.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully knows that all verbal karma is erroneous karma; he knows that all karmas are empty and non-existent, neither produced nor arisen.”
Why is this? Among all karmas, not a single one is fixed; the cessation of all karma is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

As for right action, one does not discriminate among karmas as being either right or wrong, because one enters into the equality of all karmas. Since one does not discriminate whether karma is right or wrong, it is therefore called right action.

Furthermore, right action means the sense of being unbound to the three realms; it is the sense of knowing and seeing according to reality. Within suchness and equality, there is no further discrimination between what is right and what is wrong.

When a bodhisattva practices such right action, because they know and see all actions as they truly are, they neither grasp nor reject any phenomena according to reality; therefore, it is called practicing right action.
Within right action there is no wrong action; because such a person knows and sees according to reality, they are said to abide in right action.
"World-Honored One!
What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully knowing that all forms of livelihood are wrong livelihood?"

Why is this? If one takes up the mark of life, the mark of dharmas, or the mark of grasping—even up to the mark of nirvāṇa, the mark of a Buddha, or the mark of the pure Buddha-dharmas—and dwells within these to practice a "pure" livelihood, all such instances are called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

Right livelihood means abandoning attachment to the necessities of life, ceasing all forms of trade, being free from conceptual discrimination and frivolous proliferation, and transcending all such proliferation; this is called right livelihood.

Within right livelihood, one no longer discriminates between what is wrong livelihood and what is right livelihood; thus, one attains all pure livelihood, and for this reason it is called "attaining pure right livelihood."
Furthermore, all forms of livelihood are fundamentally unarisen and devoid of either the perverse or the correct; such a person is said to have attained a pure livelihood.

Abiding securely in the right path, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they dwell within this right livelihood without grasping at right livelihood or abandoning perverse livelihood; therefore, it is called "dwelling in right livelihood."

At that time, such a person is neither said to abide in the correct nor said to abide in the deviant; they attain a pure and equal life-force (*jīvitendriya*), free from the characteristics of life-force, unmoving and unconditioned. They do not think of life-force, nor do they think of non-life-force; they are simply called one who knows according to reality and sees according to reality. For this reason, they are said to abide in the correct life-force.
“Lokadhara! What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who well understands right diligence, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva who abides in right diligence?
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of severing all paths of diligence, is said to abide in right diligence.”
Why is this? All forms of diligence are erroneous; whatever is initiated, whatever is performed, and whatever is practiced are all termed erroneous. Why is this?
All phenomena are produced erroneously; whatever is brought forth is false, and that which is false is likewise erroneous.
One who practices right diligence has no arousal, no activity, no practice, and no aspiration, having severed all purposeful action within all phenomena.

This bodhisattva has severed the notion of "something to be done" regarding all dharmas; even within the marks of nirvāṇa and the marks of a buddha, they do not give rise to the mark of something to be done. This person well understands that all that is done is entirely false and illusory; because there is nothing to be done, they practice the path in this manner.
That which is correct involves no intentional action; all phenomena are equal and without distinction, being free from the activity of acting and the marks of having acted.
This Bodhisattva skillfully knows that diligence is not the path of diligence, for it neither grasps nor rejects; thus it is called abiding in correct diligence.
Right effort is the meaning of the non-apprehensibility of all efforts; it is the meaning of knowing and seeing all phenomena as they truly are.
One who sees right effort in this way no longer discriminates between what is wrong effort and what is right effort; therefore, it is called right effort.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful knowledge of right mindfulness?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva knows and sees that all thoughts are wrong thoughts, and that whatever object is thought of is a wrong thought.”

Why is this? All thoughts are wrong thoughts; if thoughts arise regarding any object or location, they are all wrong thoughts. To be without recollection and without thought is called right mindfulness.
Why is this? All thoughts arise from false causes and conditions; therefore, wherever thoughts arise, they are all erroneous thoughts.

If there is no arising and no ceasing within any location, this is called right mindfulness. When there is no activity of thought arising within any location, this is called abiding in pure mindfulness, wherein erroneous thoughts do not arise anywhere.
This person knows and sees that all phenomena are false; within this True Dharma there is no conceptualization. For this reason, it is said that they dwell securely in right mindfulness.

Furthermore, regarding right mindfulness, one does not make distinctions among phenomena as being "right mindfulness" or "wrong mindfulness. This person penetrates the fact that all states of mind are characterized by non-mindfulness; because they constantly practice the six kinds of equanimity, they are said to dwell in right mindfulness.
This person has nothing further to crave or delight in, nor do they discriminate that this is "non-thought"; rather, through the equality of all phenomena, they penetrate all thoughts.

Because this person knows and sees all thoughts as they truly are, whether it be thought or non-thought, there is neither grasping nor abandoning; therefore, it is said that they dwell securely in right mindfulness.

What this person contemplates no longer discriminates between these as equal or unequal; regarding thought and non-thought, they neither follow nor take them as objects. Because there is no objectification, they know that all thoughts are non-thoughts; whether thought or non-thought, they no longer abide in the mind.

Because this person dwells securely in right mindfulness, they are ineffable and unindicatable; they have severed all speech and are detached from all speech. Knowing all speech as it truly is, they do not discriminate between "this" and "that," and for this reason they are said to dwell securely in right mindfulness.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in right concentration?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that all concentrations are, in fact, wrong concentrations.”

Why is this? Within all phenomena, any fixed characteristic of the object apprehended, any fixed characteristic of the cognition that apprehends, and any fixed characteristic of the conceptual proliferation of samādhi—all these are termed "erroneous."

"Deviant" has the meaning of greedy attachment; this [samādhi] is certainly not so. As for the grasping of signs or the non-grasping of signs within the object of focus—being without seeking, without conceptual proliferation, and without recollection—is called right concentration.

If one is not greedily attached and does not discriminate between "this" and "that," severing attachment to joy and not relishing the flavor of concentration, destroying the grasping at the signs of concentration so that the mind dwells nowhere—this is called right concentration.

Furthermore, as for right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*): it does not rely upon any state of meditative absorption and is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One penetrates the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) as it truly is; being well-versed in the characteristics of concentration, the mind does not become attached to them. Desiring to break through the notions of "this" and "that," one does not even differentiate such speech, because all discrimination has been severed. Therefore, it is called right concentration.

Furthermore, within right concentration, one no longer gives rise to thoughts of either the heterodox or the orthodox; because all thoughts are shattered, all thoughts are severed, and all thoughts are extinguished, it is called right concentration.

As for right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*): it does not give rise to the dualistic notions of "wrong" or "right," nor does it differentiate between wrong and right; this is called right concentration. Why is this?

Because this bodhisattva has mastered the skillful means of all concentrations and dwells within this right concentration; he is no longer bound by either concentration or the characteristics of concentration. Having transcended all characteristics of concentration, it is therefore called right concentration.

Right concentration is defined as being free from conceptual proliferation regarding phenomena; within the equality of all phenomena, there is no conceptual proliferation, such as "this is right" or "this is wrong.
Right concentration is precisely the meaning of the equality of all phenomena.
