Right Concentration is that which can emerge from all meditative absorptions and all conditioned phenomena within the three realms, and can know and see, according to reality, the meaning of birth and death within all five destinies.
“World-Holder!

This is called the skillful means for attaining right concentration when all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in such a samādhi; it is called being skilled in knowing the path and skilled in the skillful means of knowing the path—namely, knowing and seeing according to reality the path that leads to nirvāṇa.”
Chapter Nine: On the Mundane and the Supramundane “Holding the World!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who skillfully knows the mundane and supramundane dharmas?
What is called the skillful means for attaining mundane and supramundane dharmas?
Holder of the World!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas correctly contemplate mundane and supramundane dharmas.
"What are the worldly dharmas?
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

'All dharmas whatsoever arise from conceptualization and discrimination, originate from inversion, and are produced by a multitude of causes and conditions. They are bound to false conditions, arise from dualistic characteristics, and are empty and non-existent—like the variegated colors of a rainbow, or like a fire-wheel that deceives ordinary people.'"
Because it has the sense of destruction, it is conventionally designated as "the world" (*loka*); thus it is called the world. All worldly phenomena are not real;

they arise from false conditions and possess the characteristic of neither being produced nor arising. They are spoken of only because of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), and because of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharma*). They are spoken of because of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). They follow the attachments of the minds of ordinary people and further follow various attachments and wrong views. Like tangled threads without a thread, like the roots of *māḍa* grass and creeping vines entangled with one another, because they correspond to perversions (*viparyāsa*), they are called worldly phenomena.
"What are supramundane phenomena?
Such mundane phenomena have, from the very beginning, been free from their true nature; this is called 'supramundane.'"

Why is this? Because the wise cannot find worldly dharmas when they seek them, nor can they find supramundane dharmas when they seek them. There is neither the mundane nor the supramundane; dwelling within this, there is no discrimination as to what is mundane or what is supramundane. It is only for the sake of the world that the supramundane is taught.
The true reality of the world is itself the supramundane.

Why is this? Because no fixed characteristic of the world can be apprehended; the characteristics of the world have been eternally empty from the very beginning. Since worldly phenomena are not determinate, the world has been a state of quiescence from the very beginning.
“This bodhisattva thus contemplates the mundane and the supramundane; they do not apprehend the mundane, nor do they crave or cling to the supramundane.
Because this person neither thinks of nor clings to the mundane or the supramundane, they do not engage in dispute with the world.”

Why is this? Because the wise person penetrates the fact that the world is a false appearance; seeing the true nature of the world, they no longer differentiate between what is mundane and what is supramundane.
Why is this? World-Holder!
"The world" is a synonym for the five aggregates of clinging; all worldly dharmas are subsumed within them.

The wise seeker does not find the aggregates (*skandha*); they do not find the nature of the aggregates, nor the place from which they come, nor the place where they abide, nor the place to which they go.

Where there are no five aggregates, twelve bases (*āyatana*), or eighteen elements (*dhātu*); where there is no discrimination and no names; where there is no nature, no marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and no activity—this is called the supramundane (*lokottara*).
“Dhāraṇīdhara!

When a bodhisattva contemplates worldly and world-transcending dharmas, they do not see the world as merging with the world-transcending, nor do they see the world-transcending as being separate from the world.”

This person does not depart from the view of the mundane to see the supramundane, nor do they depart from the view of the supramundane to see the mundane; this person no longer takes as an object the two modes of practice, namely, "this is the mundane" and "this is the supramundane."
Why is this? World-Holder!

The true mark of the world is itself the supramundane. Within the world, the marks of the world cannot be apprehended; within worldly dharmas, worldly dharmas cannot be apprehended. Because they are non-existent, to penetrate these dharmas is itself the supramundane.
“Holder of the World!

If the mundane were different from the supramundane, the Buddhas would not appear in the world, nor would the Buddhas teach that all worlds are unobtainable and that all worlds are unborn, knowing and seeing all worlds as they truly are.”
“Dhāraṇīdhara! If one does not grasp at the world and does not take up the world, this is precisely the supramundane.
Therefore, you should know that knowing and seeing the world as it truly is—because one penetrates the fact that the world is unattainable—is what is called the supramundane.”

Therefore, when the Buddhas appear in the world, because they realize all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane—with non-duality and non-conceptualization through their knowledge and vision of reality as it is, this is precisely what is called teaching the supramundane Dharma.
“Lokadhara! Thus, this world is profound and its bottom is difficult to reach.

Those who rely on worldly dharmas, those who have attained worldly dharmas, those who long for supramundane dharmas, those who conceive the mark of the ultimate truth within conventional speech, and those who abide in dualistic dharmas—none of these can enter into such a dharma.”
Why is this? Because these people do not know the mundane world, nor do they know the supramundane; they all practice dualistic dharmas.
Holder of the World!
Those who practice two dharmas cannot penetrate the mundane and the supramundane.
Holder of the World!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva thus skillfully knows the mundane and supramundane dharmas, and also attains the skillful means regarding mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Chapter Ten: On Conditioned and Unconditioned Dharmas. *The Scripture on Holding the World*, Chapter Ten: On Conditioned and Unconditioned Dharmas. "Holding the World!
What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who skillfully knows conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and thereby attains the skillful means regarding conditioned and unconditioned dharmas?"
“World-Upholder!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas correctly contemplate and discern conditioned and unconditioned dharmas.
What is meant by correct contemplation and discernment?”

These conditioned phenomena have no agent and no experiencer; these conditioned phenomena arise by themselves and fall into the category of enumeration by themselves, and for this reason they are called "conditioned phenomena."
These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) proceed through the conjunction of false causes and conditions.
How is it that they proceed and fall into the category [of phenomena]?

Because they are known by means of two marks as objects of cognition, they are called the arising of conditioned phenomena. These phenomena have no agent (*kartṛ*) and no instigator; these phenomena arise of themselves and there is no one capable of causing their arising. For this reason, they are called conditioned phenomena.

"These conditioned phenomena do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between; they are neither joined nor dispersed. Arising from the root of false discrimination and due to the causal conditions of ignorance, they are all non-existent."
It is solely by the power of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that they possess utility; yet these dharmas have no agent and no originator. This is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
"Conditioned" carries the meaning of being bound, as it is spoken of according to the attachments of the delusions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The wise person penetrates and does not apprehend conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor do they apprehend those phenomena subsumed under the conditioned; because they are not reckoned among the categories of the wise, they are called "conditioned phenomena. Why is this?

The wise do not engage in the conceptualization of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); it is only for the sake of worldly conventional designations for ordinary people that they conceptualize the conditioned as existing.

The noble ones (*ārya*) do not follow the names and categories of any phenomena; because the noble ones are detached from the names and categories of all phenomena, it is said that those who have attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called noble ones.

"The wise person penetrates the realization that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are in fact unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, they no longer initiate the performance of various karmas.

The wise person knows and sees that the arising characteristics of all conditioned phenomena are deceptive and mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, they no longer initiate the production of the conditioned."
Why is this? Conditioned phenomena possess no fixed nature; all conditioned phenomena are without intrinsic nature and without arising or activity. Why is this?
“Lokadhara!

There is no practicing conditioned phenomena as a condition that can lead to the penetration of the unconditioned; one who has penetrated the unconditioned no longer takes conditioned phenomena as a condition.
What is meant by ‘penetration’?”

The wise person sees that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely false and illusory; they have no root and nothing to which they are attached, and they do not fall within the categories of enumeration. When observing them in this way, one no longer craves the conditions of the conditioned, nor does one grasp at conditioned phenomena.
Why is this? World-Holder!
One does not attain the unconditioned apart from the conditioned, nor does one attain the conditioned apart from the unconditioned; the suchness of the conditioned is itself called the unconditioned.

Why is this? Within the conditioned there is no conditioned, and within the unconditioned there is no unconditioned. It is only for the sake of sentient beings who are associated with inverted views that, in order to cause them to know and see conditioned phenomena, one discriminates and speaks of "this is a conditioned phenomenon" and "this is an unconditioned phenomenon," or "this is the characteristic of the conditioned" and "this is the characteristic of the unconditioned."
In this context, what are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
They are birth, cessation, duration, and change.
What are the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

"What is called 'neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor changing' refers to the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned; it is spoken only for the sake of guiding ordinary beings.
Worldly Sustainer! "

Conditioned phenomena have no characteristic of arising, no characteristic of ceasing, and no characteristic of abiding-and-changing; therefore, it is said that the characteristics of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing are themselves without characteristics and are non-arising.

If conditioned phenomena were necessarily possessed of these three characteristics, the Buddha would have definitively stated: "Such a characteristic is arising," "such a characteristic is ceasing," and "such a characteristic is abiding-and-changing."
Dhāraṇīśvara!
Just as the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are without marks.
Dhāraṇīśvara!

If non-arising were to have a characteristic, if non-ceasing were to have a characteristic, or if non-abiding-and-changing were to have a characteristic, the Buddha should have definitively described them as the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) were characterized by marks and possessed of verbal expression, it would not be unconditioned, because it would possess the nature of being expressible through marks.

However, it is merely because of conventional enumeration that ordinary beings speak of the three characteristics of the conditioned—namely, arising, ceasing, and the alteration of abiding—and the three characteristics of the unconditioned—namely, non-arising, non-ceasing, and the absence of the alteration of abiding.”
“Holder of the World!

If a person thoroughly penetrates and knows the conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, that person will no longer undergo birth, cessation, abiding, or change; for this reason, it is said that they have attained the unconditioned.”
“Holder of the World!
Arising and ceasing is precisely the meaning of seeing accumulation and disappearance.
If a dharma has no accumulation, then there is no disappearance; if accumulation does not arise, then there is neither retrogression nor abiding-change.”
"Holder of the World!
This is called the knowledge and vision of conditioned phenomena as they truly are.
If a person knows and sees conditioned phenomena as they truly are, they do not fall into the reckoning of what are called arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing."

When a bodhisattva contemplates conditioned and unconditioned phenomena in this way, they do not perceive conditioned phenomena as conjoined with unconditioned phenomena, nor do they perceive unconditioned phenomena as conjoined with conditioned phenomena.
One should simply maintain this thought:
"The true mark of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is itself the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Then, one will no longer engage in further conceptual discrimination.
If one does not discriminate between conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, that itself is the unconditioned.
If one discriminates between what is conditioned and what is unconditioned, then one cannot penetrate the unconditioned.

To sever all conceptual discrimination is called penetrating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Because one penetrates the nature of conditions as they truly are and thereby severs all conditions, one abides neither in the numerical nor in the non-numerical.
“World-Holder!

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful means regarding conditioned and unconditioned dharmas; that is to say, they do not dwell in nor are they bound to any dharmas, and they do not greedily grasp at them, whether they be conditioned or unconditioned dharmas.”
Chapter Eleven: On Past Deeds, from the *Lokadhara-sutra*. “Lokadhara!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus skillfully know the five aggregates (*skandha*), skillfully know the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), skillfully know the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*), skillfully know the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), skillfully know the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), skillfully know the five faculties (*indriya*), skillfully know the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), skillfully know mundane and supramundane dharmas, and skillfully know conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, they shall attain skillful knowledge of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas. They will also skillfully discern the phrasing, terminology, and chapters of all dharmas, and will attain the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*). By means of this power of mindfulness, they will transform their rebirth to achieve uninterrupted mindfulness, until they finally attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
“Holder of the World!

In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Jambūnada-suvarṇa-Sumeru-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
“Holding the World!
This Buddha, the King of Mountains Sumeru of Jambūnada Gold, has a lifespan of five kalpas and possesses an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas.

His buddha-field is pure, adorned, prosperous, joyful, and peaceful; its sentient beings are fully endowed with happiness, have little greed, anger, or delusion, and are easy to transform, easy to deliver, and easy to purify.”
"World-Upholder!
This Sumeru-King Jambūnada-Gold Buddha also preached for the sake of all bodhisattvas this Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra entitled 'Severing the Doubts of Sentient Beings.'"
“Holder of the World!

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Ratnaprabha who, upon hearing these skillful means regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; conditions; the four foundations of mindfulness; the five faculties; the eightfold noble path; mundane and supramundane phenomena; and conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, immediately gave rise to diligence and did not produce a single evil thought for two billion years.”

Whether it be desire, hatred, or delusion; whether it be gain, food and drink, or robes and bowls—solely for the sake of entering such gates of skillful means regarding these dharmas, one should always exert oneself with diligent vigor.
“Dhāraṇīdhara!

This Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, in the presence of the Buddha Jambūnada-suvarṇa-Sumeru-rāja, constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya) for the remainder of his life. After his death, he was reborn among humans in that same Buddha-field.”
Upon the end of his life as a youth, he was immediately reborn in the presence of that Buddha and practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Throughout each eon, he underwent five hundred births and deaths until, finally, he was born at the time when the Buddha Jambūnada-suvarṇa-Sumeru-rāja was about to enter parinirvāṇa.

"In the fifth kalpa, having accomplished such extensive learning of the Dharma and attained such skillful means regarding the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), he was able to remember all the teachings he had heard from the Buddhas. Because he had attained such power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), he addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Please allow me to expound upon these various dharmas in detail.'"
Thereupon, within that very world, he delivered and liberated immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to abide in the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"When the Tathāgata Jambūnada-suvarṇa-Sumeru-rāja enters parinirvāṇa, for the sake of upholding the Dharma, he will protect and mindfully sustain the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall remain for one kalpa; during this kalpa, for five hundred lifetimes, this person will always be born among humans, renounce the world to study the Path, and will also constantly cause the true reality (dharmatā) of these dharmas to increase within themselves, while further benefiting immeasurable and boundless sentient beings."
“Dhāraṇīdhara!

This Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, having thus successively encountered ten trillion Buddhas, was finally granted a prediction by the Buddha Amitābha, who declared: ‘After an incalculable number of kalpas, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”

Throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he further encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* Buddhas. Subsequently, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and became a Buddha named Sarvārthaniścita-vyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

There was an assembly of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattvas and an immeasurable community of śrāvakas; the Buddha’s lifespan was two kalpas, and his buddha-field was prosperous, peaceful, secure, and universally adorned.
“Holder of the World!

Therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes to attain such skillful means within these dharmas, they should practice with diligent vigor and earnestly seek them, reading, reciting, and cultivating these teachings.”
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to attain such skillful means regarding all dharmas, he practices with diligent vigor within four dharmas.
What are these four?
First is leaving the household life; second is practicing alone; third is maintaining pure precepts; fourth is eliminating the mind of indolence—these are the four.
When a bodhisattva possesses these four dharmas, diligently seeking extensive learning and abiding in patience, they shall swiftly encounter these four dharmas.

What are the four? First, being born in Jambudvīpa; second, encountering a Buddha; third, practicing in accordance with the Dharma; and fourth, eliminating the karmic obstacles of sinful deeds. These are the four.
"Furthermore, Lokadhara!

Within these dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice with diligent vigor; they shall thereby attain the power of pure giving, pure morality, pure patience, pure diligence, pure meditative concentration, and the power of pure wisdom. Abiding in these dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva swiftly attains such power of skillful means."
"Furthermore, Lokadhara!

Although a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the subtle dharmas of *dhūta*, they are also able to maintain great compassion for sentient beings at all times. Such a person enters into this mind of great compassion and exerts diligent effort within these skillful means of the Dharma."
“Holder of the World!
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain such dharmas, they should enter the gates of the dhāraṇīs and practice with diligent vigor.
What is meant by practicing with diligent vigor for the sake of entering the gates of the dhāraṇīs?

This refers to skillfully observing the immeasurable conditions of all phenomena, observing the immeasurable skillful means of all phenomena, and also observing the arising of immeasurable skillful means.

When observing in this way, through the skillful means of the gate of samādhi, one skillfully enters the immeasurable conditions of all dharma-gates, enters immeasurable skillful means, and also enters the arising of immeasurable skillful means.

Because they have gained power within this Dharma, they well understand the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; they also skillfully distinguish all literary expressions, phrases, and sentences; they further attain the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*), and achieve the dharma of non-retrogressive, uninterrupted mindfulness upon rebirth, until finally attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Lokadhara!

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter the gates of all dhāraṇīs, they penetrate the causes and conditions of all phenomena according to their suitability; by means of a single cause and condition, they can enter a thousand kinds of causes and conditions, attaining the skillful means of all phenomena through the power of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Lokadhara!
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva exerts diligent effort within these dharmas, they enter the samādhi of the single-gate of characteristics (*ekalakṣaṇamukha-samādhi*).
Having attained the samādhi of the single-gate of characteristics, they enter the samādhi of the immeasurable-gate of characteristics (*apramāṇalakṣaṇamukha-samādhi*)."
Having thus entered, by means of various causes, conditions, and skillful methods, they are able to enter these gateways to all dharmas.
Once these bodhisattvas have entered all gateways to all dharmas, they shall attain skillful means regarding all dharmas.
"Furthermore, World-Upholder!

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice wisdom extensively, they skillfully know the characteristics of all meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) and also skillfully know the objectless samādhi (anālambana-samādhi)."
By the power of this samādhi, he is able to skillfully know the arising of immeasurable meditative concentrations from immeasurable conditions.
Abiding in this stage, this bodhisattva is able to attain the skillful means regarding the true mark of all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Lokadhara!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly contemplate the conditions and skillful means of the world; they constantly contemplate the conditions and skillful means of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); they constantly contemplate the conditions and skillful means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and they also constantly and diligently practice the conditions and skillful means for the disintegration and dispersal of all phenomena, remaining without any attachment."
When this bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates such dharmas, they swiftly attain the skillful means for the true mark of all dharmas.
Furthermore, World-Holders!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva diligently practices with vigor and gives rise to the power of skillful means, while also constantly contemplating the true mark of all dharmas; they do not rely on worldly pleasures, nor do they engage in mixed conduct with worldly dharmas.

One who accomplishes such dharmas will swiftly attain the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas; they will also skillfully discern the phrasing, terminology, and chapters of all dharmas; they will obtain the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), and will attain the transformation of the body to accomplish uninterrupted mindfulness, until finally attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Holder!
Therefore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the further shore of such dharmas as these, they should practice these dharmas according to how they have been taught.”
“World-Holders!
You should practice with diligent perseverance within this Dharma; before long, you shall attain unimpeded wisdom regarding this Dharma.
World-Holders!”

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Immeasurable Light Virtue High King (*Amitābhaguṇocchrayarāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The lifespan of this Buddha, Immeasurable Light Virtuous High King, is one kalpa.
His buddha-land is covered above by nets of the seven treasures, and the world is universally adorned with many *tāla* trees made of the seven treasures.
These many *tāla* trees were likewise covered above by nets of the seven treasures, and beneath each tree was spread a lion throne.
From all the *tāla* trees issued celestial garments, and all the thrones were fashioned from lapis lazuli, Jambūnada gold, and red pearls.

On all four sides of the *tāla* trees, there were fragrant trees and flowering trees that surrounded and adorned them; beneath each tree was a pond, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.

All the ponds are composed of crystal, musaragalva, and red pearls; upon the waters of all the ponds, blue, red, white, and pink lotuses completely cover the surface; and all the ponds are surrounded by railings made of the seven treasures.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra! That Buddha-land is adorned with such multitudes of precious jewels throughout the world-system.

On its four sides there are further jewel-trees, like the Pārijātaka and Kālapriya-dhāra trees of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; such jewel-trees, numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis, surround the world-system.”
The radiance of these jewel trees eclipsed all the light of the sun and moon so that they no longer appeared.
"Sustaining the World!
From the many tala trees and the various jewel nets, various kinds of wondrous sounds spontaneously issued forth."
Like the sounds of songs sung by celestial maidens, such subtle and wondrous sounds constantly emerge from that buddha-field.
There are no three evil realms, nor even the names of the three evil realms.
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

This Buddha Immeasurable Light Virtuous High King extensively expounds such teachings for the sake of all sentient beings—namely, the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra that Severs All Doubts of Sentient Beings and Gladdens the Hearts of All Sentient Beings.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

When the Buddha Immeasurable Light Virtuous High King preached the Dharma, within a single day, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and those who had so resolved all attained the complete fulfillment of the factors conducive to enlightenment.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!

By these causes and conditions, the Buddha Immeasurable Radiance Virtuous High King has taught and brought to fulfillment immeasurable and boundless sentient beings in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In that Buddha-land, the number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly great.”
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma remained for half an eon.

At the time when the Dharma was about to perish after the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha Immeasurable Light Virtuous High King, ten Buddha-worlds below there was a bodhisattva named Immeasurable Intention.”
Having passed away from his previous life, he was reborn at the age of sixteen and left the household life to study the Way.

At a time when the Buddha-dharma of the King of Immeasurable Radiant Virtue was about to perish, he heard this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva expounding the *Sūtra on the Expedient Means of the Aggregates, Elements, and Sense-bases*.

Having heard this sutra, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Intention (Amitābha-mati) gave rise to great diligence; therein, he reached the ultimate limit of this Dharma and accomplished profound power of skillful means.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, at the end of his life there, he encountered twenty billion buddhas and attained the accomplishment of such dharmas as these.

He constantly remembered his past lives, left home in the state of a *kumārabhūta*, and practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). He always possessed the power of mindfulness and was never separated from such dharmas in successive lifetimes. In every birth, he achieved uninterrupted mindfulness, and thereafter attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, becoming the Buddha named Immeasurable Light Adornment King (*Amitābhavyūharāja*).
“World-Holder!

Therefore, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to swiftly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, or wishes to swiftly attain the full realization of all-encompassing wisdom, they should, during the five hundred years of the evil age after my parinirvāṇa, diligently protect and uphold [the Dharma] by making great vows; they should give rise to great desire, great diligence, and great heedfulness, and throughout future ages, they must constantly protect and uphold sūtras such as these.”
At that time, the bodhisattvas, with Bhadrapāla and Garāhuda as their leaders, rose from their seats and joined their palms toward the Buddha.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, we shall protect such sūtras as these; we shall practice with diligent vigor, reading, reciting, listening to, and receiving them, and we shall also extensively expound them for others."
Furthermore, several thousands of bodhisattvas rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, gazed up at his venerable countenance, and made this aspiration:
“World-Honored One!

In future ages, during the final five hundred years, we make this vow: regarding such profound and undefiled teachings of the Buddhas, which can give rise to all the wholesome merits of a bodhisattva and can fulfill all the factors conducive to enlightenment for a bodhisattva, we shall together protect and uphold them upon hearing such Dharma; we shall purify our minds with great clarity and joy, and with single-minded diligence, seek to receive, maintain, read, and recite them.
The Buddha then smiled, and immediately immeasurable light filled the trichiliocosm, while the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition do you now smile and the great earth tremble?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see these bodhisattvas who have made great vows to protect and uphold such a profound and undefiled Dharma in future ages?"
Ānanda! These bodhisattvas have not only made this vow in the present life. Ānanda!

I recall that these bodhisattvas, in the presence of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, made such vows to protect and uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time, and were likewise able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

Now, you shall likewise protect and uphold my Dharma during the three periods—namely, in the present, after my parinirvāṇa, and when the Dharma is about to perish—and thereby bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
"Holder of the World!

Just as Bhadrapāla and others have protected and upheld my Dharma during the three periods, they shall likewise protect and uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas during the three periods within this Bhadrakalpa, and they shall also protect and uphold such a Dharma during the three periods in the presence of all future Buddhas."
“Ānanda! I now praise and speak of this person’s accomplishment of such immeasurable merit as being inexhaustible; they act out of compassion for sentient beings, bringing them benefit and peace.”
Ānanda! If I were to fully describe all such merits of this person, people would be unable to believe it.
If a person does not believe the Buddha’s words, that person will lose their benefit for a long night, undergoing various sufferings and falling into the evil destinies.

“Ānanda! I have now roughly described how these bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings. Suppose there were as many sentient beings as would fill a trichiliocosm, and they all fell into the great earth hells.
Among them, one person said to the sentient beings:
"Do not be afraid; I shall now, one by one, undergo this suffering of the great hell on your behalf.
That person immediately led the sentient beings out of hell, and for each of them, he underwent the sufferings of hell for many tens of millions of years.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Would this person not achieve great benefit and great peace and happiness?
Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!
It will bring great benefit and great peace and happiness.”
“Ānanda! After these people have delivered all sentient beings, they manifest their power and influence, causing them all to attain the foremost happiness in the world.”
"Ānanda! Is such a person able to be gracious and able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
The benefit brought by this person cannot be described in words.
“Ānanda! [The Buddha replied.]

I now truly declare that the Bodhisattvas Bhadrapāla, Garuḍa, Hārītīputra, and others who benefit sentient beings, and these people who benefit sentient beings—between these two kinds of beneficial and blissful deeds, no calculation or analogy can serve as a comparison.
Why is this? Ānanda!

These requisites for pleasure are all conditioned phenomena that are contrary [to liberation]; they do not lead to disenchantment, nor to the fading away of desire, nor to wisdom, nor to the fruits of the śramaṇa, nor to nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! These bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings by bestowing upon them unsurpassed happiness; they perform the work of a Buddha for all those who seek the path to Buddhahood with joy. They cause those who have not yet entered the stage of certainty to attain the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they transform, instruct, benefit, and gladden the bodhisattvas through the Buddha-dharma.”

Ānanda! These bodhisattvas are able to instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden the assembly of bodhisattvas; they abide in the world for the sake of not severing the lineage of the Buddhas and for the sake of guarding the seed of omniscience.

“Ānanda! When this person was originally practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, he ensured that there were always Buddhas and never allowed the lineage to be severed; likewise, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas in the future, he shall ensure that there will always be Buddhas and never allow it to be severed.”
Why is this? Ānanda!

When these bodhisattvas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they had already caused immeasurable Buddhas to abide in the Buddha-way; throughout their successive lives, these bodhisattvas have protected, sustained, taught, and transformed hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, causing them all to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

From this time forward, they shall likewise transform and guide countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Buddha-way; through the power of their transformation, these beings will become fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma and shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

“Ānanda! These, such as Bhadrapāla and the others, practice with diligent vigor for the sake of bestowing upon sentient beings the bliss of the Buddha and the bliss of all-encompassing wisdom. Ānanda!”
If someone were to ask in truth:
"Who are the parents, the saviors, the shelter, the refuge, the island, and the source of birth for all bodhisattvas?
the bodhisattvas should reply: "They are these five hundred bodhisattvas, such as Bhadrapāla, Garuḍa, and so forth."
“Ānanda! If someone were to ask in truth:
‘What is the seed of all bodhisattvas?’”
"One should say that it was Bhadrapāla, Garāhādaṭa, and the others, five hundred in all.
Such sons of good family as these dwell in the world for the sake of not severing the lineage of the Buddhas and not severing the lineage of all-encompassing wisdom."

These sons of good family, likewise, in future ages during the final five hundred years, by the power of these skillful means of teaching and transformation, shall cause all sentient beings not to fall into the three evil realms through the conditions of happiness, and shall also cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
“Ānanda! Even if thousands of Buddhas were to speak of the merits of these sons of good family, they could not exhaustively describe them. Why is this?
These sons of good family have accomplished such inconceivable merit. Ānanda!

The treasury of Dharma that I have accumulated over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas—these sons of good family are able to receive, protect, and uphold it.

Ānanda! I now entrust to these people this Dharma-treasure accumulated over immeasurable billions of kalpas. These sons of good family and others shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas currently residing in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya lands.
“Ānanda! These sons of good family are worthy of being honored and served by all the world, including its devas and humans. Ānanda!”
"This person is constantly praised by the thousand Buddhas of the ten directions when they preach the Dharma.
Ānanda! I have already certified this for the sake of severing the doubts of all sentient beings."

If, in the final age at the end of time, there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and extensively expound this sutra for others, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family are close to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, if anyone in the final age at the end of time even hears such a profound sutra as this, believes and understands it, and gives rise to a vow, I shall grant them all the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If, in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there are good sons or good daughters who give rise to a mind of faith and understanding, and who diligently practice with vigor to protect and uphold this sutra, I now likewise entrust them with this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If a śrāvaka person believes and accepts such a profound Dharma with a mind free from opposition, I shall grant them a prediction that they will, in the future, encounter the assembly of Maitreya Buddha.

If those who seek the Buddha-way hear such a Dharma as this and receive, uphold, believe, and understand it, all these people shall be granted a prediction of enlightenment by Maitreya Buddha; by virtue of their original vows, they shall leave the household life to study the Way.

Ānanda, you should know that if these sons and daughters of good family, in a future age during the final five hundred years, practice with diligent perseverance within this Dharma, you should know that the roots of goodness of such persons are fierce and sharp.
Chapter Twelve: Entrustment. From the *Lokadhātṛ* Sūtra, Chapter Twelve, the Chapter on Entrustment. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lokadhātṛ addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I pray that, for the sake of benefiting all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, you will protect and keep this sutra in mind.
If, in future ages, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear this Dharma and their minds are purified with joy and delight, they shall also practice with diligent vigor in order to fully realize such a Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, mindful of this sutra, immediately employed his supernatural power to cause the fragrance to pervade this trichiliocosm, such as had never been experienced before, so that all sentient beings directed their hearts toward one another with loving-kindness.
Having thus protected and remembered him, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvara: "Dhāraṇīśvara!
I now protect and remember this *Dharmamudrāparivarta Sūtra* in order to sever all doubts."
"World-Holder!
If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they shall before long attain all-encompassing wisdom, with the sole exception of their original vows.
I now likewise bestow upon such persons a prediction of enlightenment, because they shall swiftly attain the full perfection of all-encompassing wisdom."

“Lokadhara! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva receives, upholds, reads, and recites this *Dharmamudrā-parivarta Sūtra*, contemplates it, and explains it extensively for others, that person shall before long swiftly attain skillful means regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), mundane and supramundane dharmas, and conditioned and unconditioned dharmas. They shall also swiftly attain the true mark of all dharmas (*sarvadharma-bhūtalakṣaṇa*), swiftly attain the analytical discernment of the chapters and phrases of all dharmas, swiftly attain the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), and swiftly attain the transformation of the body to achieve uninterrupted mindfulness, until they finally attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Holder of the World!

In future ages, this sutra will be able to act as a great Dharma illumination and a light of great wisdom for sentient beings, serving as a cause and condition for merit; it will also be able to provide all bodhisattvas with the complete dharmas that assist in attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Dhāraṇīdhara!

If, in the final age of the future, there are bodhisattvas who encounter this sutra and other profound sutras included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka that correspond to the various pāramitās, such persons will not be obscured by the deeds of Māra, nor will they be afflicted by karmic obstructions.”
“Holder of the World!

If this person has not yet attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), I grant them this prediction: in a future age, under the second and third Buddhas, they shall attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena.”

Those who have already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena will swiftly attain the power of mastery over all dharmas, swiftly attain a pure buddha-field, swiftly attain an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas, and swiftly attain an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas.
“World-Upholder!
I now proclaim this Dharma-seal for the purpose of severing all doubts regarding future lives.
World-Upholder!”
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see four benefits, they make vows to protect and uphold sūtras such as these in the future final age.
What are these four?
The bodhisattvas form this thought: "I shall swiftly attain immeasurable and boundless merit;

I shall also cause sentient beings to give rise to great roots of goodness; I shall act as a guardian of the True Dharma for all Buddhas; I shall become a person who upholds the treasury of the Dharma for all Buddhas; and I shall be seen and praised by immeasurable Buddhas."
"These are called the four.
World-Holder!
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see four benefits and thus make vows to protect and uphold this sutra in the future final age."
What are the four? All bodhisattvas form this thought:
"In order to protect the Dharma in the future, terrifying, and evil age, we shall practice great diligence."
In the future evil age when the True Dharma is being destroyed, you will be able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma; this is a difficult task.
In that future evil age, amidst the chaos of the Dharma and the confusion of sentient beings, we shall protect the Dharma so that our minds remain undisturbed;
at that time, we shall attain perfect patience and protect the Dharma through the path of non-anger.
"These are called the four.
World-Holder!
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see these four benefits, they protect and uphold such profound sūtras as these, making vows in the future evil age."
The five hundred bodhisattvas, including Bhadrapāla and Garaghatada, as well as other bodhisattvas, having heard this Sūtra on the Chapter of the Dharma-Seal, joined their palms before the Buddha.
To those who, in the future evil age, make a vow to protect and uphold this profound Dharma, the Buddha will stroke their heads with his right hand and speak these words:
"O sons of good family!..."

The great Dharma-treasury of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have accumulated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, is exceedingly difficult to assemble; it has involved undergoing immeasurable and boundless sorrow, grief, and suffering, as well as relinquishing immeasurable and boundless joy and happiness.

I now entrust this to you all: in the future, during the final age, you should skillfully open up for others this treasury of Dharma accumulated over immeasurable kalpas; extensively analyze and explain this seed of the True Dharma for the fourfold assembly so that it shall not be severed, and you yourselves must once again kindle the great torch of the Dharma.
"O sons of noble family!

The Tathāgata now requests you, my disciples, to abide where the Buddhas abide, so that I may widely proclaim and disseminate for all devas and humans this treasury of the Dharma-jewels accumulated by me over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
Thereupon, Bhadrapāla, Garaghaṭṭa, and the others immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke thus:
“To the extent of our own capabilities, and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, we shall widely proclaim and disseminate this treasury of the Dharma-treasure in future ages.”

When this *Dharmamudrā-parivarta Sūtra* was being preached, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) perfected their roots of goodness;

likewise, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and were all destined to receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara, Bhadrapāla, Garaghatada, and the others, along with the other bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, as well as all the devas, humans, asuras, and so forth, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
